papers.paper_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Transfer from freshman definitions to organic chemistry
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the freshman-chemistry electron-transfer definition of oxidation/reduction transfers directly and intuitively to organic chemistry without reinterpretation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In organic chemistry, oxidation and reduction are often identified by changes in bonding patterns and electron density, not only by simple ion-electron bookkeeping.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that organic redox can be described by changes such as loss/gain of hydrogen, addition/loss of oxygen, or changes in electron density around carbon, and then relate those changes back to electron accounting when appropriate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the application of this knowledge is not intuitively transferable in organic chemistry"
misconceptions.population: Beginning students in introductory organic chemistry
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think reduction of a carbonyl is just 'hydrogenation' or addition of hydrogen, without recognizing the electron-transfer step.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbonyl reduction involves gain of electrons by the carbonyl carbon, with protonation occurring afterward to give the reduced product.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first identify the electron gain at carbon, then see protonation as a separate step that neutralizes charge and completes product formation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the 'actual reduction step' ... because each carbon gains one electron (a total of two). The last stage is merely the acquisition of two protons"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the metal reduction of a carbonyl is a single direct hydrogenation rather than an electron donation from the metal followed by protonation/workup.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc first donates electrons to the carbonyl-derived intermediate; protonation then completes the reduction to the methylene product.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track electrons from Zn^0 to the substrate, then account for added H+ in the workup as the final protonation step that gives the neutral product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Zinc metal (oxidation state 0) provides the electrons that actually effect the reduction"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Alcohol intermediate as part of reduction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not realize that converting the putative alcohol intermediate to the methylene group is itself a reduction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Both the carbonyl-to-alcohol stage and the alcohol-to-methylene stage involve reduction steps in the overall Clemmensen reduction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare oxidation states/electron density at carbon across the steps and see that each step corresponds to further reduction of the carbon center.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the conversion of the putative alcohol intermediate to the methylene group is also a reduction"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the Wolff–Kishner reduction is only a reduction of the carbonyl-derived carbon and overlook that the nitrogen atoms are oxidized.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The Wolff–Kishner reaction is an internal redox/disproportionation in which carbon is reduced and nitrogen is oxidized to N2.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should assign electrons/oxidation states across the hydrazone and see that one part of the molecule loses electron density (nitrogen to N2) while carbon gains it.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one portion (the nitrogens) is oxidized and the other portion (the carbon) is reduced"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation of elemental nitrogen within hydrazone
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may find it counterintuitive or implicitly believe the nitrogens are not oxidized because they are being removed as N2.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrogen atoms in the hydrazone are oxidized because they end up in molecular nitrogen after losing electron density in the process.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow electron sharing: nitrogen atoms in the hydrazone are bonded in a way that differs from elemental nitrogen, and formation of N2 reflects oxidation of those nitrogens.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it is somewhat more difficult to accept that the nitrogens are oxidized"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think reduction does not occur until the quench/workup step with acid or water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction has already occurred when hydride attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon and delivers electrons; workup only protonates the intermediate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the hydride as a proton plus two electrons, recognize electron transfer to the substrate during nucleophilic attack, and treat quenching as a separate finishing step.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the reduction has occurred already!"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the catalyst itself is the reducing agent or that the reduction is caused by a 'reduced catalyst' being transferred to the double bond.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen adsorbs on the catalyst surface and then hydrogen atoms/electrons are delivered to the substrate; the catalyst is not the species being reduced in the product-forming step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the catalyst surface as a site for H2 activation from the actual transfer of hydrogen to the alkene, which causes reduction of the substrate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "transfer of this 'reduced catalyst' (hydrogenated catalyst) to the double bond"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think reduction requires a distinct 'nascent hydrogen' species rather than equivalent electron/proton accounting from common hydrogen sources.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Whether hydrogen comes from Zn/HCl, hydride plus workup, or H2, the essential redox accounting is delivery of electrons and protons that reduce the substrate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate each reagent set into electrons plus protons and see that different practical sources of hydrogen can represent the same net reduction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many of these reductions are called 'reduction with nascent ... hydrogen'"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may equate oxidation of alcohols only with loss of oxygen or dehydrogenation, rather than with electron loss / increased oxidation state of carbon.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Alcohol oxidation can be understood as loss of electrons from carbon and decreased electron density, often accompanying loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the structural change to electron accounting: carbon loses electron density when bonded to more electronegative atoms or when C-H bonds are replaced by C=O.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the alcohol was 'dehydrogenated' or oxidized"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think only methyl ketones undergo the haloform reaction and overlook that secondary methyl carbinols are first oxidized to methyl ketones in situ.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Secondary methyl carbinols can also undergo the reaction because the reagents oxidize the alcohol to the ketone before haloform cleavage occurs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize the alcohol-to-ketone oxidation step under halogenation conditions and not restrict the reaction only to pre-existing methyl ketones.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "secondary methyl carbinols are also subject to this conversion since the reagents oxidize them to methyl ketones in situ"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not realize that halogen radicals can each take one electron from both the C-H bond and the O-H bond during oxidation of alcohols.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The oxidation proceeds through electron transfer from the substrate to the halogen radicals, generating a carbonyl group, halide ions, and protons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should trace how electrons move from the alcohol to the halogen species and infer the oxidation of the carbon center from the resulting product and electron balance.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the halogen radicals ... can acquire one electron each from the carbon–hydrogen bond and the oxygen–hydrogen bond"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Bond polarity and ownership of bonding electrons
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation/reduction must always be described as literal electron loss/gain and not as changes in electron density around atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation can be understood more broadly as decreased electron density and reduction as increased electron density around the atoms involved.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider electronegativity and how bonding electrons are shared differently after substitution or functional-group change, then infer whether electron density increases or decreases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "classify oxidation as a decrease of electron density and reduction as an increase of electron density"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to see that converting an alkane carbon to an alcohol or alkyl halide is oxidation because no formal charge change is shown.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Replacing C-H bonding with C-O or C-Br bonding decreases electron density at carbon because oxygen and bromine are more electronegative than hydrogen.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the electronegativities of atoms bonded to carbon and recognize that sharing electrons with a more electronegative atom makes the carbon more oxidized.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the carbon goes from sharing the pair of electrons ... with the less electronegative hydrogen to sharing it with the more electronegative oxygen ... or bromine"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not recognize epoxidation of an alkene as an oxidation because the carbon skeleton still looks similarly bonded.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Epoxidation is oxidation because the alkene carbons share their pi electrons with more electronegative oxygen, decreasing electron density at carbon.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should treat the pi electrons as being redistributed toward oxygen and conclude that the alkene carbons become more oxidized.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When the alkene is epoxidized, these electrons are now shared with the more electronegative oxygen"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not see that a gem-dihalide is more oxidized than a monohalide and that this can be comparable to a carbonyl oxidation level.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Additional halogen substitution increases oxidation level; a gem-dihalide is more oxidized than a monohalide and can be at the same oxidation level as a carbonyl group.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the carbon’s bonding partners across the series and use electron density/oxidation-state reasoning to order the compounds by oxidation level.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the carbon of a gemdihalide ... is at the same oxidation level as the carbonyl group"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Benzyl alcohol to benzoic acid sequence
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may treat the sequence benzyl alcohol → benzaldehyde → benzoic acid as unrelated transformations rather than a progression of increasing oxidation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: This sequence is an oxidation progression characterized by loss of hydrogen and gain of oxygen, corresponding to decreased electron density at carbon.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify each step as increasing oxidation level by tracking the bond changes from alcohol to aldehyde to carboxylic acid.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the sequence going from benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde then to benzoic acid labeled 'loss of hydrogen' (–2H) and 'gain of oxygen' (+O) are indeed understandable in terms of 'decreased electron density'"
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.subtopic: Memorization as a substitute for understanding
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may believe oxidation–reduction in organic chemistry is something to memorize blindly because it seems foreign and unrelated to freshman chemistry.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should use coherent electron-density and electron-accounting reasoning to connect organic redox transformations to familiar redox definitions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should build a conceptual bridge between general redox and organic redox instead of relying on rote memorization.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "mystery and blind acceptance (i.e. memorization) out of the sheer instinct of 'self-preservation'"
misconceptions.population: one student quoted by the author
misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

papers.paper_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic composition of copper(II) sulfate solution
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw copper(II) sulfate in water as molecules rather than as ions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution dissociates into ions, not neutral molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that an aqueous ionic compound separates into constituent ions in solution and represent those ions at the particulate level.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Drawing copper(II) sulfate in water as molecules not as ions"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of product on the metal surface
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the solid deposition on zinc metal as precipitation of zinc sulfate (a molecular precipitate).
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the zinc–copper(II) sulfate reaction, copper metal deposits on zinc; zinc sulfate remains in aqueous ionic form.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track which species are reduced and oxidized, recognize that copper ions gain electrons to form copper atoms, and distinguish a solid metal deposit from dissolved zinc sulfate ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Drawing zinc sulfate as molecular precipitate, that is to say, identifying and indicating solid deposition in solution as the precipitation of zinc sulfate"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not show zinc ions going into solution.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc atoms oxidize to zinc ions, and those zinc ions enter the aqueous solution.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow the oxidation half-process at the particulate level: zinc atoms lose electrons and become aqueous zinc ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Not drawing zinc ions going into solution"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not discriminate atoms and ions in the reaction process.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and ions are different particle types and must be distinguished when describing oxidation and reduction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify whether a species is neutral or charged, and use that distinction to describe electron transfer and changes in particle identity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Not discriminating atoms and ions involving reaction process"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe spectator ions deposit on the metal surface to form a precipitate.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Spectator ions remain in solution and do not precipitate onto the metal surface in the zinc–copper(II) sulfate reaction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which ions actually participate in the redox change and which remain unchanged in solution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "After identifying a common alternative conception, which was the deposition of spectator ions on the metal to form a precipitate"
misconceptions.prevalence: Identified in the pilot study as the common alternative conception used to design the inaccurate animation; exact number not provided.
misconceptions.population: Pilot study with another group of 13 senior preservice chemistry teachers (12 interviewed)
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Copper(II) sulfate species in the inaccurate animation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think copper and sulfate are bonded together as molecules in solution rather than ionized.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution is dissociated into ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from electrolyte behavior and ionic notation that the dissolved species are ions, not intact molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it shows copper and sulphate together, as if they were bonded, as if they were not ionized in the solution."
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in interview commentary; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.population: Preservice chemistry teachers (at least one participant with scientific understanding)
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer partner in the incorrect animation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons move from zinc atoms to sulfate ions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are transferred from zinc metal to copper(II) ions, not sulfate ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should match oxidation with the species that loses electrons and reduction with the species that gains electrons, using the reaction stoichiometry and ionic charges.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "electron transfer from zinc atoms to sulfate ions"
misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later recognized as wrong by participants; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Product assignment in the incorrect animation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think zinc sulfate precipitates onto zinc atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc sulfate does not precipitate here; zinc ions go into solution and copper metal deposits on the zinc surface.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the aqueous product from any solid deposit and track the ionic exchange correctly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "formation and deposition of zinc sulfate precipitate on the zinc atoms"
misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later refuted by participants; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.subtopic: Direction of copper movement in the incorrect animation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think copper atoms are released into solution.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) ions gain electrons and deposit as copper metal on the zinc surface; they do not leave as neutral copper atoms into solution.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow reduction: copper ions in solution gain electrons and become solid copper at the surface.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "releasing of copper atoms into the solution"
misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later refuted by participants; exact count not provided.
misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students focus only on symbolic charge changes such as 2+ to 0 and 0 to 2+ without understanding how particles move at the molecular level.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions should be understood through electron transfer and the corresponding particulate changes in atoms, ions, and metal deposition/dissolution.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect symbolic oxidation states to actual particle transformations: zinc atoms oxidize to zinc ions and copper ions reduce to copper atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "we learned the phenomenon mathematically focusing on the charge changes in ions; for example, it changes from (2+) to (0), or it changes from (0) to (2+). I have never thought how these entities move at the molecular level."
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported by one participant with alternative understanding.
misconceptions.population: 1 preservice chemistry teacher with alternative understanding
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students expect the animation to show color change directly at the submicroscopic level and do not connect the fading blue color to fewer copper ions in solution.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The observed color change at the macroscopic level corresponds to a decrease in copper(II) ions at the particulate level.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the blue color of copper(II) sulfate solution to the presence of copper ions and infer that fewer copper ions mean a paler color.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the color of zinc [atoms] gets darker, so what is depositing must be zinc."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in one moderate-understanding participant; broader pattern noted among several students, exact count not provided.
misconceptions.population: Preservice chemistry teachers, including 1 with moderate understanding
misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

papers.paper_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer / oxidation state / ionic charge
misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction means loss of electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is gain of electrons; in half-reactions, the reduced species gains electrons and usually its oxidation state decreases.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which reactant gains electrons in the equation; that species is reduced, and its oxidation number decreases as a consequence of electron gain.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "reduction half-reaction involves loss of electrons"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction is identified by decrease in oxidation state caused by loss of electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction involves gain of electrons and often a decrease in oxidation state; the decrease is the result of electron gain, not electron loss.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check electron flow first: the species that gains electrons is reduced; then confirm that its oxidation number decreases because of the gained electrons.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because  $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$  losses electron and became  $\text{Cr}^{3+}$  which made it reduction half reaction"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction is determined by a decrease in ionic charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is determined by gain of electrons, which may change oxidation number; ionic charge is not the same as oxidation number in all species.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electron transfer and oxidation number rules, not just compare charges, to decide which half-reaction is reduction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "reduction half-reaction involves reduction in ionic charge"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves decrease in oxidation number.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and corresponds to an increase in oxidation number.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine that the species losing electrons is oxidized, and its oxidation number should rise rather than fall.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reactions involve decrease in oxidation number"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves gain of electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons; the oxidized species donates electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate the species that loses electrons in the reaction and identify that as the oxidation half-reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reactions involve gain of electrons"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves loss of oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation can be defined by electron loss and increase in oxidation number; oxygen transfer is only one model and not always applicable.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not assume oxygen is always being removed or added; instead they should track electrons and oxidation number in the balanced equation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reaction involves loss of oxygen atoms"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction is defined by removal of oxygen and increase in oxidation state as if both were the same criterion.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons with increase in oxidation number; oxygen removal may be related in some reactions but is not the defining criterion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify oxidation by electron loss and oxidation-number increase, independent of whether oxygen appears in the species.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reaction involves removal of oxygen and increase in oxidation state"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves gain of electrons to increase oxidation state.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and increase in oxidation state.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that gaining electrons lowers oxidation state, so a species that gains electrons cannot be the one oxidized.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half is the gain of electrons. That is there is an increase in oxidation state of Mg from 0 state to +2 state"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves gain of ionic charge or increase in ionic charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation involves loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number, not merely change in ionic charge.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the electron transfer and oxidation number change; an increase in charge does not by itself define oxidation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Mg has gain a charge of +2 in Mg^{2+}"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves decrease in ionic charges.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation involves loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number; charge changes must be interpreted using electron transfer, not as a standalone rule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether electrons are lost or gained before deciding oxidation or reduction, rather than using charge decrease alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because zinc has reduced the charge of +2 to zero (0) charge"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves increase in ionic charges.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number, not simply any increase in charge.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should link oxidation to electron loss and oxidation-number increase, and avoid equating every charge increase with oxidation without checking the equation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}; because of the charge in the reactant has increased"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves gain of electrons and oxygen atoms together as the criterion.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number; oxygen transfer is only one possible model and should not be mixed indiscriminately with electron transfer.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the correct model for the reaction and not infer oxidation from a combination of unrelated features like both oxygen and electron gain.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} is the answer because Mg gained electrons and also oxygen was added"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is oxidised because its oxidation number decreases.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A species is oxidised when it loses electrons and its oxidation number increases.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check which species loses electrons; that species is oxidized and its oxidation number goes up.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Cl_2 is oxidised as there is a decreased in its oxidation number"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is oxidised because it accepts electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons; the oxidised species donates electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify electron donation as oxidation, not electron acceptance.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the answer is Br because it accepts an electron to become Br_2"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is oxidised because it contains oxygen atoms or gains oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation may involve oxygen in some cases, but the general definition is loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not classify a species as oxidized just because oxygen is present; they should examine electron transfer and oxidation number.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "ZnSO_4; this is because there is an increase in oxygen. Oxidation is defined as the gain of oxygen"
misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is oxidised because it loses oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Loss of oxygen can be one model, but oxidation is fundamentally loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should decide based on electron loss/oxidation-number increase, not just oxygen loss.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Cu is oxidised because it decreased in the number of oxygen atoms"

misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidising agents accept electrons and are reduced.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine which species gains electrons and is reduced; that species is the oxidising agent.

Conception, threshold concept, and troublesome knowledge in redox reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the charge on a polyatomic ion or molecule is itself the oxidation number.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation number is a formal accounting value assigned to atoms in compounds or ions; it is not the same as the overall charge of a polyatomic ion or molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the oxidation number of each atom by applying oxidation-number rules and not equate the net ionic charge with oxidation state. They should distinguish the total charge of an ion from the oxidation number of an element within that ion.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: students experiencing misconceptions that assume the charge on polyatomic ions, are oxidation numbers
misconceptions.prevalence: 31.4% of first-semester students; 28.2% of second-semester students
misconceptions.population: First-semester and second-semester students (Brandriet and Bretz study cited in the paper)
misconceptions.source_title: Conception, threshold concept, and troublesome knowledge in redox reaction

misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation and reduction identification using charge change
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe any change in the charge of a polyatomic or molecular ion indicates oxidation or reduction of that species.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction are identified by changes in oxidation number due to electron transfer, not by changes in the net charge of a species.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare oxidation numbers of the relevant atoms before and after the reaction and determine whether electrons are lost or gained. Net charge changes alone do not define oxidation or reduction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: changes in polyatomic ion and molecular ion charges can be used to identify the species of oxidation and reduction reactions
misconceptions.population: Students in studies cited by the paper (including Schmidt and Volke; Brandriet and Bretz; Garnett and Treagust)
misconceptions.source_title: Conception, threshold concept, and troublesome knowledge in redox reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electron transfer occurs when the bond between a cation and a spectator ion breaks or forms, rather than between the reacting species themselves.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer is the actual movement of electrons from the reducing agent to the oxidizing agent during the redox process; it is not caused by simple breaking or forming of an ionic bond in the written equation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species that lose and gain electrons and explain transfer at the particulate level. They should not infer electron movement merely from bond breaking or bond formation between ions in a formula equation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: electron transfer occurs when the bond between the cation and the spectator ion breaks/ forms
misconceptions.prevalence: 69.7% of first-semester students; 68.6% of second-semester students
misconceptions.population: First-semester and second-semester students (Brandriet and Bretz study cited in the paper)
misconceptions.source_title: Conception, threshold concept, and troublesome knowledge in redox reaction

misconceptions.subtopic: Using charge change to assign oxidation/reduction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students conclude that if a species changes from one charge to another, that species must be oxidized or reduced, even when the change is only in net ionic charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation/reduction must be assigned from oxidation-number change and electron transfer, not from charge change of species like nitrate, carbonate, or carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the oxidation number of the atom undergoing change and determine whether it increases or decreases. They should not assign oxidation state changes based solely on the overall charge written on the species.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: students assume changes in charge in polyatomic ions could be used to identify specific oxidation and reduction reactions
misconceptions.population: Students in Germany and other students described in the cited studies

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain the blackening of heated copper as ash deposition, combustion, or a direct heat-induced color change of copper atoms rather than a redox process.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The black color is produced by a redox reaction involving oxidation of copper, leading to formation of a new substance on the copper surface.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the macroscopic observation to a submicroscopic explanation and recognize that heating copper in air produces oxidation products rather than mere physical color change or ash contamination.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students decide whether a reaction is redox mainly from the visible form of the equation or reaction type label, rather than from changes in oxidation numbers or electron transfer.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction is classified as redox by determining whether oxidation numbers change and/or electrons are transferred.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect reactants and products, compare oxidation numbers of the relevant species, and decide redox status from the change in oxidation state, not from superficial features such as the equation looking like a combination reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This shows that the concept of redox reactions understood by this preservice chemistry teacher is not good enough, because it can be confused by looking at the reaction equation displayed."

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a charge is the number of valence electrons and an oxidation number is the number of bonding electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Charge and oxidation number are different concepts; oxidation number is an assigned bookkeeping number for atoms in compounds, not the number of bonding electrons, and charge is not the number of valence electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine the oxidation number by applying oxidation-number rules to the atom in its chemical context, and distinguish that from the actual ionic charge or electron counts.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a redox reaction can be described simply as zinc and copper swapping places, rather than by oxidation and reduction occurring through electron transfer and oxidation-number changes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the Zn/Cu redox reaction, zinc is oxidized and copper ions are reduced; the correct explanation is based on oxidation-number change and electron transfer.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the species before and after reaction, identify which species loses electrons and which gains electrons, and explain the reaction by oxidation-number changes rather than by merely saying substances exchanged positions.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if a reaction is a combination reaction, then that is the reason it is not redox or the main explanation for the reaction type.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction may be redox if oxidation numbers change, regardless of whether it is also a combination reaction.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oxidation and reduction cannot both occur if there is only one product in the reaction.

misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes for oxygen and hydrogen in water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assign oxidation numbers in water simply as oxygen changing from 0 to -2 and hydrogen from 0 to +1, treating the changes as if they follow from the image without a proper rule-based explanation.

misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide is reduced because of glaring light in the furnace.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reduction of iron oxide is caused by chemical reaction with carbon/CO under high-temperature conditions, not by light itself.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should focus on reactants and electron transfer rather than unrelated visible features like light intensity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “iron oxide has reduced; because the iron is running out with glaring means, the iron oxide has reduced” (182).

misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
misconceptions.target_misconception: Carbon is the main reason iron oxide is reduced because a catalyst increases the rate of every reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon in the blast furnace is a reactant/reducing agent, not merely a catalyst; the reaction chemistry must be explained by redox processes.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that a catalyst is not consumed and does not determine product identity, whereas carbon is oxidised while iron oxide is reduced.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “carbon was a catalyst; because addition of a suitable catalyst increases the rate of every reaction” (011).

misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
misconceptions.target_misconception: A redox reaction occurs because electrons are removed from a substance, without identifying which species loses or gains them.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should identify the oxidation as electron loss by carbon/CO and reduction as electron gain by iron species in the blast furnace.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students need to specify the transferring species and connect electron loss with oxidation and electron gain with reduction in the overall redox reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred because of the removal of an electron from a substance has occurred” (083).

misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide decomposes into elements because coal is heated with it.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blast furnace reaction is a redox reduction, not simple decomposition into elements.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not infer decomposition from heating alone; they should explain the conversion of iron oxide to iron through reduction by carbon/CO.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat oxidation and reduction of organic compounds as movements of hydrogen only, rather than as changes in oxidation state that can also involve oxygen and other heteroatoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction in organic chemistry are determined by changes in oxidation state, often reflected by loss/gain of hydrogen and gain/loss of oxygen or other electronegative atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine bond changes and determine whether the carbon atom's oxidation state increases or decreases. Loss of H or gain of O/X increases oxidation state; gain of H or loss of O/X decreases oxidation state.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Oxidation is the loss of hydrogen... Reduction is the gain of hydrogen..."

misconceptions.subtopic: Assuming oxidation always means adding oxygen and reduction always means removing oxygen
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation is only the addition of oxygen and reduction is only the removal of oxygen, ignoring other valid indicators such as hydrogen loss/gain or oxidation state changes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction can be recognized by changes in oxidation state; oxygen transfer is only one possible pattern, alongside hydrogen transfer and changes in bonding to electronegative atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the oxidation state of the carbon center before and after reaction, not rely only on oxygen addition/removal. If the oxidation state increases, the compound is oxidized; if it decreases, it is reduced.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Oxidation is the gain of oxygen... Reduction is the loss of oxygen..."

misconceptions.subtopic: Judging oxidation/reduction solely from numbers of bonds to oxygen or hydrogen
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may equate oxidation or reduction with simple bond-count rules only, such as counting C-O, C-H, or C-C bonds, rather than reasoning in terms of oxidation state changes at carbon.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond counting is useful only insofar as it helps determine carbon oxidation state; the real criterion is whether the oxidation state increases or decreases.

More bonds to oxygen or fewer bonds to hydrogen generally indicate oxidation, but the underlying concept is oxidation state change.

misconceptions.subtopic: Thinking oxidation and reduction are simply changes in hydrogen or oxygen counts without oxidation state analysis
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may treat redox in organic chemistry as a bookkeeping problem of adding/removing H or O only, rather than determining whether carbon is oxidized or reduced by changes in oxidation number.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox classification depends on oxidation state: oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation/reduction is only about explicit electron transfer and not about the structural changes that define oxidation state changes in organic compounds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In organic chemistry, oxidation and reduction are commonly inferred from changes in bonding to H, O, N, halogens, or C, which correspond to changes in oxidation state and electron density.

misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic observation of iron in copper(II) sulfate
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron does not react with CuSO4 / is insoluble in CuSO4, or that the visible change means iron simply dissolves like sugar in water rather than undergoing redox.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron displaces copper from CuSO4; the reaction is a redox process in which iron is oxidized and copper(II) is reduced, producing a reddish solution / copper deposit.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the observed color change to electron transfer and recognize that Fe(s) reacts with Cu2+(aq) to form Fe2+(aq) and Cu(s), rather than interpreting the observation as simple dissolution or no reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students with ability levels (-1.5 to 1.5 logit) are more dominant choosing the answer distractor B option (Iron does not react with CuSO4 solution)."
misconceptions.population: 1150 11th grade students from eight senior high schools in Eastern/Northern Sulawesi, Indonesia
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic observation of iron in copper(II) sulfate
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron is insoluble in CuSO4 because it is hard/solid, so they infer no chemical reaction from the visible evidence.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron undergoes oxidation in the reaction with CuSO4; the reaction is chemical, not dissolution based on hardness or physical appearance.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not infer reactivity from the physical hardness of iron; instead they should reason from the chemical changes and product formation expected in a displacement redox reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "iron is insoluble in CuSO4, due to the hard properties of iron."
misconceptions.population: Low-ability students in the macroscopic reasoning item analysis
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the net ionic equation can be written as Fe(s) + Cu(aq) → Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s), treating copper as neutral Cu(aq) instead of Cu2+ and/or omitting the ionic charge change.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct net ionic equation is Fe(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify copper in solution as Cu2+ ions, then conserve charge and atoms while showing electron transfer from Fe to Cu2+.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students with low ability levels ... tend to choose the answer distractor C (Fe2+(s) + Cu(aq)→ 2Fe(aq) + Cu(s)) and B (Fe(s) + Cu(aq)→ Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s))."
misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron accepts electrons from CuSO4 instead of donating electrons to Cu2+.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron is oxidized by losing electrons; Cu2+ is reduced by gaining those electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track electron flow from Fe to Cu2+ and conclude that Fe is the electron donor and Cu2+ is the electron acceptor.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students with abilities ranging from -1.5 to 1.0 logit, tend to choose A (iron accepts electrons from CuSO4)."
misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi(Q2)
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the reaction between iron and CuSO4 is a redox reaction because of a generic idea of reaction occurrence, rather than because of electron transfer and oxidation-state changes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is redox because Fe is oxidized and Cu2+ is reduced through electron transfer.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the electron-transfer model to justify redox classification, not merely the fact that two substances react.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students with low ability levels (less than - 0.5 logit) tend to choose C option (reaction of iron and CuSO4 is a redox reaction)."
misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi(Q2)
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think zinc undergoes reduction when its oxidation number changes from 0 to -2.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc is oxidized in the reaction with CuSO4; its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers to reactants and products, then determine that Zn loses electrons and therefore its oxidation number increases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students' misconceptions, especially in understanding the changes in oxidation number of Zn (from 0 to -2), Zn experiences reduction."
misconceptions.population: Low-ability students in the symbolic reasoning analysis of item 6skBb
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students select oxidation-state options that place Zn or sulfate in incorrect oxidation states, showing confusion about how to assign oxidation numbers in the reaction equation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq), Zn goes from 0 to +2 and Cu2+ goes from +2 to 0; sulfate remains a spectator ion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers consistently to each species in the equation and identify only the species that actually change oxidation state.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This fact shows the students' weak understanding regarding the concept of oxidation number."
misconceptions.population: Students in the analysis of item 6skBb(Q2)
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Identifying the reducing agent in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think CuSO4 solution is the reducing agent in the reaction with zinc.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc powder is the reducing agent because it is oxidized and donates electrons; Cu2+ is reduced.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the species that loses electrons as the reducing agent and link that to the oxidation of Zn to Zn2+.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students argue that the reducing agent in the reaction between Zn and CuSO4 is a solution of CuSO4."
misconceptions.population: Students in the analysis of item 7skBs(Q1)
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Identifying the reducing agent in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse the role of products and reactants by thinking CuSO4 is the product of zinc undergoing reduction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: CuSO4 is a reactant providing Cu2+; it is not the product, and zinc is the reducing agent.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should classify substances by their role in the reaction equation and determine which reactant is oxidized and which is reduced.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper (II) sulphate is product of Zincthat undergo reduction"
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students write the rusting reaction as 4Fe + 3O3 → 2Fe2O3 instead of using oxygen gas O2.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct reaction is 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the correct chemical formula of molecular oxygen and balance the rusting equation accordingly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "34% of students stated the reaction of iron rusting is 4Fe + 3O3→ 2Fe2O3"
misconceptions.population: Students in the item 13D response-pattern analysis
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the metal is reduced and oxygen is oxidized in rusting.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron is oxidized and oxygen is reduced in the rusting reaction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers before and after reaction to determine that Fe loses electrons and O gains electrons.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "48% of students stated that the metal was reduced and oxygen was oxidation."
misconceptions.population: Students in the item 13D response-pattern analysis
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the reaction AgNO3 + KCl → AgCl + KNO3 is a reduction reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: This reaction is a non-redox precipitation reaction; there is no electron transfer or oxidation-number change.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should check oxidation states of all species and see that they remain unchanged, so the reaction is not redox.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "25% of students stating that the reaction of AgNO3 + KCl→ AgCl + KNO3 is a reduction reaction"
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the precipitation reaction AgNO3 + KCl → AgCl + KNO3 involves oxidation-number change and electron transfer.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is not redox; it is a double displacement/precipitation reaction with no oxidation-state change.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare oxidation numbers before and after the reaction and recognize they do not change, so electron transfer is absent.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "33% of students have reason that there is a change in oxidation number and electrons transfer in the reaction."
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Autoredox reaction of chlorine in water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO is a redox reaction in the generic sense of electron transfer, without recognizing it as an autoredox reaction of the same substance.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is an autoredox (disproportionation) reaction because chlorine is simultaneously oxidized and reduced.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should see that the same element, chlorine, undergoes both oxidation and reduction in the reaction, so it is classified as autoredox.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "44% of students are sure that the reaction: Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO is a redox reaction, and 30% of students have reason that the reaction occurs because there is electrons transfer."
misconceptions.prevalence: 44%; 30% gave the electron-transfer reason
misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

papers.paper_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a reaction is redox only if oxygen is involved, and reject electron-transfer redox reactions that do not contain oxygen.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions can be defined by electron transfer, and oxygen transfer is only one special case.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify redox by asking whether electrons are transferred or oxidation states change, rather than whether oxygen is present in the reactants.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "MgO and Mg(OH)2 contain oxygen, what is absolutely necessary for redox reactions; to any redox reaction "O" is necessary – so choice (i) cannot be a redox reaction".
misconceptions.prevalence: about half of the students chose the correct answer (i); the remaining participants were not sure and chose (ii) or (iii) or both
misconceptions.population: several thousand secondary education students (Schmidt, 1994); cited in the paper
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic surface observation interpreted as sticking/gluing
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain the copper-colored coating on an iron nail as copper sulfate sticking, gluing, staining, or hanging on the nail like paint or wood color drying.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The copper coating forms because copper ions in solution are reduced to copper atoms that deposit on the iron while iron is oxidized into ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the visible coating to microscopic particle changes: copper ions gain electrons and become copper atoms that plate out, while iron loses electrons and enters solution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper Sulphate sticks on the nail; it stuck, it glues on the nail like colour on a piece of wood and then dries up".
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students attribute the red copper deposit to attraction or magnetism caused by the iron nail.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The deposit forms through electron transfer and redox chemistry, not magnetic attraction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that iron reduces copper ions in solution; the deposit results from chemical reduction, not physical attraction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Half of the students suspected an attraction as the cause of the red substance; other substance, other students mentioned an existing magnetism – probably because of the iron nail."
misconceptions.prevalence: Half of the students suspected an attraction; other students mentioned magnetism
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Misuse of scientific terms without correct redox meaning
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can say things like copper dissolves, binds to iron, or copper atoms attract electrons, while still not correctly understanding the redox process.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should use scientific terms consistently with the particle model: copper ions are reduced to copper atoms, and iron is oxidized.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not just insert technical vocabulary; they need to explain electron gain by copper ions and electron loss by iron atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper dissolves from the sulphate and binds to the iron; Copper Sulphate is reduced: Copper atoms attracts electrons; iron nails can absorb the ionic solution".
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Black coating on heated copper is soot rather than copper oxide
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the black outside layer on heated copper is soot from combustion/fire rather than an oxide layer formed by reaction with oxygen.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating copper in air forms copper oxide on the outside surface; this is a redox reaction involving oxidation of copper.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the black coating to copper reacting with oxygen in air, not to soot from burning, and should recognize oxidation of copper to oxide.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "by the flame/through combustion/fire is formed soot, burns outside the copper plate, copper oxidizes, the soot is copper II oxide".
misconceptions.prevalence: 59% chose option B; only 21% gave the right answer (C)
misconceptions.population: students in the study on grades 10–12
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Combustion products explained as everyday-life soot/carbon products
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think oxygen is 'burned' and soot or carbon products are deposited, producing several everyday-life combustion products rather than a single oxidation product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper is oxidized by oxygen; the process should be explained as a redox reaction with electron transfer / oxidation of copper, not as soot formation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the particle-level idea that oxygen in air oxidizes copper, forming copper oxide, and not invent combustion products like CO, CO2, or C as separate deposits.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxygen is burned and soot is deposited; oxygen is burned and carbon IV oxide is produced, the combustion leads to three products: CO, CO2, C".
misconceptions.prevalence: Many students
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Carbon as catalyst in blast furnace reduction
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think carbon only acts as a catalyst or heat supplier and does not actually react in the blast furnace.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon is a reducing agent; it reacts with oxygen from iron oxide and is oxidized while iron oxide is reduced to iron.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that carbon removes oxygen from iron oxide, so carbon is consumed and oxidized rather than merely helping the reaction or supplying heat.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Carbon only helps to get the reaction going, but it does not react, carbon supplier the heat is necessary for the decomposition of iron oxide".
misconceptions.prevalence: Mostly the answer (A) was chosen; correct answer (B) was only given by 20%
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron oxide simply decomposes into elements when heated with carbon.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The process is a redox reaction in which iron oxide is reduced by carbon to iron, while carbon is oxidized.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify that oxygen is transferred from iron oxide to carbon, leading to reduction of the oxide and oxidation of carbon, not simple decomposition.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "carbon supplier the heat is necessary for the decomposition of iron oxide".
misconceptions.prevalence: The correct answer (B) was only given by 20% of the students
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Writing balanced redox equations and half-reactions
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are unable to write correct equations for redox reactions, determine which species is oxidized or reduced, determine oxidation states, or write balanced oxidation/reduction half-reactions correctly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should determine oxidation states, identify electron loss and gain, and balance redox equations and half-reactions using conservation of mass and charge.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track electrons and oxidation numbers systematically to decide what is oxidized/reduced and then balance the half-reactions accordingly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Common areas of misconceptions include the students' inability to write the correct equation for reaction, determination which species is oxidized or reduced, determine the oxidation state of the species involved in the reaction, write a balanced equation for the reduction and oxidation half reaction correctly, or balance correctly a given redox equation."
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

misconceptions.subtopic: Metal and ion level confusion in copper plating example
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students describe redox at the substance level rather than at the particle level, e.g., saying 'one Copper two ions takes two electrons and is reduced to Copper' without correctly linking it to copper atoms/ions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox should be described at the submicroscopic level: copper ions gain electrons to become copper atoms, and metal atoms lose electrons to become ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish macroscopic substances from particles and explain reduction as copper ions gaining electrons to form copper atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one Copper two ions takes two electrons and is reduced to Copper": (instead of "to one Copper atom").
misconceptions.population: students at the beginning of their studies in chemistry
misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

papers.paper_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Outer valence electrons are not part of a metal atom and do not affect its size.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Valence electrons are part of the atom/ion and contribute to its apparent size.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that the outer electron cloud belongs to the atom; if electrons are lost or gained, the size of the species should change accordingly because the electron distribution changes.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the misconception that the valence electrons are not part of the atom was seen in student comments"
misconceptions.prevalence: 6 students had difficulty interpreting whether the size of the metal atoms should include the transparent light grey sphere
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.subtopic: Valence electrons as forces or bonds
misconceptions.target_misconception: The valence electrons in a metal represent molecular forces or bonds rather than electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The transparent fuzzy region represents valence electrons, not a force or bond.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the visual cue as an electron cloud around the metal atoms, and distinguish electrons from the interactions that hold the metal together.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Maybe that is supposed to represent the forces that make it a solid."
misconceptions.prevalence: 17 students
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: The red/white shapes represent nitrate ions, so nitrogen atoms are drawn as red and oxygen atoms are drawn as white.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The red/white shapes are water molecules in the more complex animation; nitrate ions are the blue/red clusters.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the key features of the animation and the chemical formula/structure of nitrate to identify species correctly rather than matching the color scheme to a remembered formula.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The nitrates. ... They are the two red with a white."
misconceptions.prevalence: 28 of 55 students
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: The blue/red clusters represent water molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blue/red clusters represent nitrate ions; water is represented by the large array of red/white shapes in the complex animation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify water by its abundant presence and molecular structure, and not confuse a nitrate ion depiction with water.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Water molecule."
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Cations and anions are attached or bonded together as ion pairs in water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When ionic compounds dissolve, the ions dissociate and exist as separate solvated ions in water.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that water stabilizes separated ions through hydration, so the ions are not permanently bonded as neutral pairs in solution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Just takes the copper [ions] and bonds it together with nitrate."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students thought ion-pairs would exist; 2 students viewing the simplified animation and 33 viewing the complex animation showed comments suggesting ion pairs
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: There are more silver ions than nitrate ions before the reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In silver nitrate solution, silver and nitrate ions should be present in equal numbers before reaction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the formula AgNO3 and charge neutrality to infer a 1:1 ratio of Ag+ to NO3-.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There is too much water. I see mostly silver not much nitrate."
misconceptions.prevalence: 14 students viewing the complex animation
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: There are more nitrate ions than silver ions before the reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver and nitrate ions should be present in equal numbers before the reaction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that silver nitrate dissociates into equal numbers of Ag+ and NO3- ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Way more nitrates than silver."
misconceptions.prevalence: 10 students
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Silver ions in this reaction have a +2 charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions in silver nitrate are Ag+ ions with a +1 charge.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the known formula of silver nitrate and charge balance to assign Ag+ rather than guessing a +2 charge.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Ten of these students believed that silver forms Ag2+ ions"
misconceptions.prevalence: 10 students
misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

misconceptions.target_misconception: Nitrate ions in this reaction have a -2 charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate ions are NO3- ions with a -1 charge.
