all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "transfer of this 'reduced catalyst' (hydrogenated catalyst) to the double bond"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think reduction requires a distinct 'nascent hydrogen' species rather than equivalent electron/proton accounting from common hydrogen sources.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Whether hydrogen comes from Zn/HCl, hydride plus workup, or H2, the essential redox accounting is delivery of electrons and protons that reduce the substrate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate each reagent set into electrons plus protons and see that different practical sources of hydrogen can represent the same net reduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many of these reductions are called 'reduction with nascent ... hydrogen'"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may equate oxidation of alcohols only with loss of oxygen or dehydrogenation, rather than with electron loss / increased oxidation state of carbon.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Alcohol oxidation can be understood as loss of electrons from carbon and decreased electron density, often accompanying loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the structural change to electron accounting: carbon loses electron density when bonded to more electronegative atoms or when C-H bonds are replaced by C=O.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the alcohol was 'dehydrogenated' or oxidized"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think only methyl ketones undergo the haloform reaction and overlook that secondary methyl carbinols are first oxidized to methyl ketones in situ.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Secondary methyl carbinols can also undergo the reaction because the reagents oxidize the alcohol to the ketone before haloform cleavage occurs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize the alcohol-to-ketone oxidation step under halogenation conditions and not restrict the reaction only to pre-existing methyl ketones.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "secondary methyl carbinols are also subject to this conversion since the reagents oxidize them to methyl ketones in situ"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not realize that halogen radicals can each take one electron from both the C-H bond and the O-H bond during oxidation of alcohols.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The oxidation proceeds through electron transfer from the substrate to the halogen radicals, generating a carbonyl group, halide ions, and protons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should trace how electrons move from the alcohol to the halogen species and infer the oxidation of the carbon center from the resulting product and electron balance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the halogen radicals ... can acquire one electron each from the carbon–hydrogen bond and the oxygen–hydrogen bond"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Bond polarity and ownership of bonding electrons
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation/reduction must always be described as literal electron loss/gain and not as changes in electron density around atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation can be understood more broadly as decreased electron density and reduction as increased electron density around the atoms involved.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider electronegativity and how bonding electrons are shared differently after substitution or functional-group change, then infer whether electron density increases or decreases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "classify oxidation as a decrease of electron density and reduction as an increase of electron density"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to see that converting an alkane carbon to an alcohol or alkyl halide is oxidation because no formal charge change is shown.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Replacing C-H bonding with C-O or C-Br bonding decreases electron density at carbon because oxygen and bromine are more electronegative than hydrogen.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the electronegativities of atoms bonded to carbon and recognize that sharing electrons with a more electronegative atom makes the carbon more oxidized.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the carbon goes from sharing the pair of electrons ... with the less electronegative hydrogen to sharing it with the more electronegative oxygen ... or bromine"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not recognize epoxidation of an alkene as an oxidation because the carbon skeleton still looks similarly bonded.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Epoxidation is oxidation because the alkene carbons share their pi electrons with more electronegative oxygen, decreasing electron density at carbon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should treat the pi electrons as being redistributed toward oxygen and conclude that the alkene carbons become more oxidized.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When the alkene is epoxidized, these electrons are now shared with the more electronegative oxygen"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not see that a gem-dihalide is more oxidized than a monohalide and that this can be comparable to a carbonyl oxidation level.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Additional halogen substitution increases oxidation level; a gem-dihalide is more oxidized than a monohalide and can be at the same oxidation level as a carbonyl group.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the carbon’s bonding partners across the series and use electron density/oxidation-state reasoning to order the compounds by oxidation level.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the carbon of a gemdihalide ... is at the same oxidation level as the carbonyl group"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Benzyl alcohol to benzoic acid sequence
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may treat the sequence benzyl alcohol → benzaldehyde → benzoic acid as unrelated transformations rather than a progression of increasing oxidation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: This sequence is an oxidation progression characterized by loss of hydrogen and gain of oxygen, corresponding to decreased electron density at carbon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify each step as increasing oxidation level by tracking the bond changes from alcohol to aldehyde to carboxylic acid.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the sequence going from benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde then to benzoic acid labeled 'loss of hydrogen' (–2H) and 'gain of oxygen' (+O) are indeed understandable in terms of 'decreased electron density'"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Memorization as a substitute for understanding
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may believe oxidation–reduction in organic chemistry is something to memorize blindly because it seems foreign and unrelated to freshman chemistry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should use coherent electron-density and electron-accounting reasoning to connect organic redox transformations to familiar redox definitions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should build a conceptual bridge between general redox and organic redox instead of relying on rote memorization.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "mystery and blind acceptance (i.e. memorization) out of the sheer instinct of 'self-preservation'"
all_misconceptions.population: one student quoted by the author
all_misconceptions.source_title: Understanding Oxidation–Reduction in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic composition of copper(II) sulfate solution
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw copper(II) sulfate in water as molecules rather than as ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution dissociates into ions, not neutral molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that an aqueous ionic compound separates into constituent ions in solution and represent those ions at the particulate level.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Drawing copper(II) sulfate in water as molecules not as ions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of product on the metal surface
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the solid deposition on zinc metal as precipitation of zinc sulfate (a molecular precipitate).
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the zinc–copper(II) sulfate reaction, copper metal deposits on zinc; zinc sulfate remains in aqueous ionic form.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track which species are reduced and oxidized, recognize that copper ions gain electrons to form copper atoms, and distinguish a solid metal deposit from dissolved zinc sulfate ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Drawing zinc sulfate as molecular precipitate, that is to say, identifying and indicating solid deposition in solution as the precipitation of zinc sulfate"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not show zinc ions going into solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc atoms oxidize to zinc ions, and those zinc ions enter the aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow the oxidation half-process at the particulate level: zinc atoms lose electrons and become aqueous zinc ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Not drawing zinc ions going into solution"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not discriminate atoms and ions in the reaction process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and ions are different particle types and must be distinguished when describing oxidation and reduction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify whether a species is neutral or charged, and use that distinction to describe electron transfer and changes in particle identity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Not discriminating atoms and ions involving reaction process"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included as an alternative-understanding criterion; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe spectator ions deposit on the metal surface to form a precipitate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Spectator ions remain in solution and do not precipitate onto the metal surface in the zinc–copper(II) sulfate reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which ions actually participate in the redox change and which remain unchanged in solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "After identifying a common alternative conception, which was the deposition of spectator ions on the metal to form a precipitate"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Identified in the pilot study as the common alternative conception used to design the inaccurate animation; exact number not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Pilot study with another group of 13 senior preservice chemistry teachers (12 interviewed)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper(II) sulfate species in the inaccurate animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think copper and sulfate are bonded together as molecules in solution rather than ionized.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution is dissociated into ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from electrolyte behavior and ionic notation that the dissolved species are ions, not intact molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it shows copper and sulphate together, as if they were bonded, as if they were not ionized in the solution."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in interview commentary; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Preservice chemistry teachers (at least one participant with scientific understanding)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer partner in the incorrect animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons move from zinc atoms to sulfate ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are transferred from zinc metal to copper(II) ions, not sulfate ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should match oxidation with the species that loses electrons and reduction with the species that gains electrons, using the reaction stoichiometry and ionic charges.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "electron transfer from zinc atoms to sulfate ions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later recognized as wrong by participants; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Product assignment in the incorrect animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think zinc sulfate precipitates onto zinc atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc sulfate does not precipitate here; zinc ions go into solution and copper metal deposits on the zinc surface.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the aqueous product from any solid deposit and track the ionic exchange correctly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "formation and deposition of zinc sulfate precipitate on the zinc atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later refuted by participants; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Direction of copper movement in the incorrect animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think copper atoms are released into solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper(II) ions gain electrons and deposit as copper metal on the zinc surface; they do not leave as neutral copper atoms into solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow reduction: copper ions in solution gain electrons and become solid copper at the surface.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "releasing of copper atoms into the solution"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Feature of the inaccurate animation, later refuted by participants; exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Inaccurate animation used with 22 senior preservice chemistry teachers
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students focus only on symbolic charge changes such as 2+ to 0 and 0 to 2+ without understanding how particles move at the molecular level.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions should be understood through electron transfer and the corresponding particulate changes in atoms, ions, and metal deposition/dissolution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect symbolic oxidation states to actual particle transformations: zinc atoms oxidize to zinc ions and copper ions reduce to copper atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "we learned the phenomenon mathematically focusing on the charge changes in ions; for example, it changes from (2+) to (0), or it changes from (0) to (2+). I have never thought how these entities move at the molecular level."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported by one participant with alternative understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: 1 preservice chemistry teacher with alternative understanding
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students expect the animation to show color change directly at the submicroscopic level and do not connect the fading blue color to fewer copper ions in solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The observed color change at the macroscopic level corresponds to a decrease in copper(II) ions at the particulate level.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the blue color of copper(II) sulfate solution to the presence of copper ions and infer that fewer copper ions mean a paler color.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the color of zinc [atoms] gets darker, so what is depositing must be zinc."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in one moderate-understanding participant; broader pattern noted among several students, exact count not provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Preservice chemistry teachers, including 1 with moderate understanding
all_misconceptions.source_title: Chapter 2 Revisiting the Understanding of Redox Reactions Through Critiquing Animations in Variance

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer / oxidation state / ionic charge
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction means loss of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is gain of electrons; in half-reactions, the reduced species gains electrons and usually its oxidation state decreases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which reactant gains electrons in the equation; that species is reduced, and its oxidation number decreases as a consequence of electron gain.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "reduction half-reaction involves loss of electrons"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction is identified by decrease in oxidation state caused by loss of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction involves gain of electrons and often a decrease in oxidation state; the decrease is the result of electron gain, not electron loss.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check electron flow first: the species that gains electrons is reduced; then confirm that its oxidation number decreases because of the gained electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because  $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$  losses electron and became  $\text{Cr}^{3+}$  which made it reduction half reaction"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reduction half-reaction is determined by a decrease in ionic charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is determined by gain of electrons, which may change oxidation number; ionic charge is not the same as oxidation number in all species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electron transfer and oxidation number rules, not just compare charges, to decide which half-reaction is reduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "reduction half-reaction involves reduction in ionic charge"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves decrease in oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and corresponds to an increase in oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine that the species losing electrons is oxidized, and its oxidation number should rise rather than fall.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reactions involve decrease in oxidation number"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves gain of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons; the oxidized species donates electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate the species that loses electrons in the reaction and identify that as the oxidation half-reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reactions involve gain of electrons"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation half-reaction involves loss of oxygen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation can be defined by electron loss and increase in oxidation number; oxygen transfer is only one model and not always applicable.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not assume oxygen is always being removed or added; instead they should track electrons and oxidation number in the balanced equation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation half-reaction involves loss of oxygen atoms"

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is oxidised because it loses electrons to change ionic charge.

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is reduced because it loses electrons.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is reduced because it loses electrons as a result of loss of oxygen atoms.

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is reduced because it is on the reactant side and its oxidation number decreases there.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction occurs for the species that gains electrons, usually shown by a decrease in oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate which species actually gains electrons in the reaction, regardless of a vague reactant/product-side rule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "ZnSO_4; because it is decreasing in oxidation number"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is reduced because it gained electrons, as if gaining electrons makes it reduced only when charge becomes positive.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is gain of electrons and typically decrease in oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that electron gain corresponds to reduction, and not confuse positive charge with electron gain.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} which means Zn has gain electron and hence is reduced"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A species is reduced because oxygen is removed from it and then it is treated as having lost electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is gain of electrons; oxygen removal may be one model but should not be used to infer electron loss incorrectly.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should directly follow the electron flow and oxidation-number change in the chemical equation.

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction should be identified by electron gain and oxidation-number decrease, not by forcing hydrogen transfer where none exists.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should only use the hydrogen model when hydrogen is actually transferred in the reaction, and otherwise use electron transfer/oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Cl^- is the answer because it gains hydrogen from the reactants to form Cl^- in the products"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reducing agents are species that accept electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reducing agents donate electrons and are oxidized.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should look for the electron donor in the reaction and identify that as the reducing agent.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Reducing agents are atoms (species) that accept electrons in reactions"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reducing agents are species with no oxygen atoms bonded to them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reducing agents are electron donors; the presence or absence of oxygen is not the definition.

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from electron transfer and oxidation-number change rather than from whether hydrogen can be accepted.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the answer is CuSO_4 because it cannot take on hydrogens because the oxidation number of Zn had increased"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Reducing agents accept electrons and lose oxygen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reducing agents donate electrons and are oxidized; oxygen loss is not the defining property of a reducing agent.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the electron donor as the reducing agent and not confuse the agent with the reduced species or oxygen loss.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Zn; addition of electrons and loss oxygen atom to a substance makes it a reducing agent"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine which species gains electrons and is reduced; that species is the oxidising agent.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "CuSO_4; because it was oxidised at the reactant side and losses it electron at the product side, thus it made the Zn oxidised which makes it an oxidising agent"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "ZnSO_4; because it received the oxygen so therefore is the oxidising agent"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify electron acceptance as the defining feature of an oxidising agent, not donation of electrons or oxygen.

all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the electron-gaining species as the oxidising agent, but must link this to reduction rather than oxidation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Br_2; it has gain electron"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidising agents are species with positive charge or species that reduce the charge of another species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An oxidising agent is a species that accepts electrons and is reduced; charge alone is not the criterion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electron transfer and oxidation state to identify oxidising agents, not just the sign of charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Cu; it has charge of positive which make it oxidising agent"

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should decide from electron gain and reduction, then use oxidation number only as support.

all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species that is reduced and recognizes that it oxidizes the other species; that species is the oxidising agent.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "ZnSO_4 is an oxidising agent in the reaction because it is reduced"
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN LEARNING OXIDATION-REDUCTION REACTIONS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe any change in the charge of a polyatomic or molecular ion indicates oxidation or reduction of that species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction are identified by changes in oxidation number due to electron transfer, not by changes in the net charge of a species.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electron transfer occurs when the bond between a cation and a spectator ion breaks or forms, rather than between the reacting species themselves.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer is the actual movement of electrons from the reducing agent to the oxidizing agent during the redox process; it is not caused by simple breaking or forming of an ionic bond in the written equation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species that lose and gain electrons and explain transfer at the particulate level. They should not infer electron movement merely from bond breaking or bond formation between ions in a formula equation.

all_misconceptions.population: First-semester and second-semester students (Brandriet and Bretz study cited in the paper)

all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation/reduction must be assigned from oxidation-number change and electron transfer, not from charge change of species like nitrate, carbonate, or carbon dioxide.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the oxidation number of the atom undergoing change and determine whether it increases or decreases. They should not assign oxidation state changes based solely on the overall charge written on the species.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students assume changes in charge in polyatomic ions could be used to identify specific oxidation and reduction reactions
all_misconceptions.population: Students in Germany and other students described in the cited studies

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Interpreting observable color change as combustion/heat effect
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain the blackening of heated copper as ash deposition, combustion, or a direct heat-induced color change of copper atoms rather than a redox process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The black color is produced by a redox reaction involving oxidation of copper, leading to formation of a new substance on the copper surface.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the macroscopic observation to a submicroscopic explanation and recognize that heating copper in air produces oxidation products rather than mere physical color change or ash contamination.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Some students' opinions about this phenomenon are that black is produced due to precipitation of ash and as a result of combustion reactions. In addition, other students think that high temperatures change the color of copper atoms to black
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 59% answered the phenomenon as a redox reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students decide whether a reaction is redox mainly from the visible form of the equation or reaction type label, rather than from changes in oxidation numbers or electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction is classified as redox by determining whether oxidation numbers change and/or electrons are transferred.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect reactants and products, compare oxidation numbers of the relevant species, and decide redox status from the change in oxidation state, not from superficial features such as the equation looking like a combination reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This shows that the concept of redox reactions understood by this preservice chemistry teacher is not good enough, because it can be confused by looking at the reaction equation displayed."

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a charge is the number of valence electrons and an oxidation number is the number of bonding electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Charge and oxidation number are different concepts; oxidation number is an assigned bookkeeping number for atoms in compounds, not the number of bonding electrons, and charge is not the number of valence electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine the oxidation number by applying oxidation-number rules to the atom in its chemical context, and distinguish that from the actual ionic charge or electron counts.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The charge states the number of valence electrons, but oxidation numbers state number of bonding electrons"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 55.00% (22/40) at level I; 42.9% (15/35) at level II; 40.00% (10/25) at level III; 46.94% (23/49) at level IV

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a redox reaction can be described simply as zinc and copper swapping places, rather than by oxidation and reduction occurring through electron transfer and oxidation-number changes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the Zn/Cu redox reaction, zinc is oxidized and copper ions are reduced; the correct explanation is based on oxidation-number change and electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the species before and after reaction, identify which species loses electrons and which gains electrons, and explain the reaction by oxidation-number changes rather than by merely saying substances exchanged positions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I feel more confident (on change) the charge. Zinc on the left 1, the right I forgot, I think it increases"

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if a reaction is a combination reaction, then that is the reason it is not redox or the main explanation for the reaction type.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction may be redox if oxidation numbers change, regardless of whether it is also a combination reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Classify the reaction by checking oxidation-state changes first; only then consider whether it is also a combination reaction as a separate reaction type, not as a substitute explanation.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oxidation and reduction cannot both occur if there is only one product in the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction can occur in the same reaction even if the equation shows one product; redox is determined by electron transfer and oxidation-number changes, not by the number of products.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Examine the oxidation numbers of atoms in reactants and products; if one species is oxidized and another reduced, the reaction is redox regardless of whether there is one product or more.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oxidation and reduction cannot occur when the reactants are uncharged.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions can occur with neutral reactants; what matters is whether oxidation numbers change and electrons are transferred.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Check the oxidation numbers of atoms in the reactants and products even when the species are neutral, and determine whether some atoms are oxidized while others are reduced.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Only one reactant means no oxidation-reduction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oxidation and reduction cannot occur when there is only one reactant.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A redox process can occur even when only one reactant is shown in the simplified representation; the key is whether atoms change oxidation state or electrons are transferred.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Analyze the submicroscopic change in oxidation numbers and electron movement rather than counting reactants; a single reactant can still be involved in a redox process if its atoms undergo oxidation-state change.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes for oxygen and hydrogen in water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assign oxidation numbers in water simply as oxygen changing from 0 to -2 and hydrogen from 0 to +1, treating the changes as if they follow from the image without a proper rule-based explanation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation numbers are assigned by oxidation-state rules based on the chemical context; in water formation/decomposition, atoms change oxidation states according to those rules, not by arbitrary image interpretation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use oxidation-number rules to track each atom in the reactant and product and explain the changes by electron transfer and formal oxidation-state assignment.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The oxidation numbers change from 0 to -2 for oxygen and from 0 to +1 for hydrogen"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 24.83% selected this alternative concept for item 6
all_misconceptions.source_title: AN ANALYSIS OF PRESERVICE CHEMISTRY TEACHERS' MISCONCEPTIONS OF REDUCTION-OXIDATION REACTION CONCEPTS

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons move from cadmium sulfate to iron, or that the bond between cadmium and sulfate breaks and iron binds to sulfate, as if electron transfer were just bond swapping.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the redox reaction, electrons are transferred between species through oxidation and reduction; cadmium sulfate in solution is ionic, and the reaction is not explained by a covalent bond-breaking/bond-forming picture.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the ionic species in solution, then trace electron loss and gain between the reacting species; explain the reaction using oxidation-number changes and electron transfer rather than bond replacement.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Cadmium sulfate electrons moved first, continued to bind to iron"

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe there is no explanation of electron transfer in redox reactions, only a change of substances or products.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions are explained by electron transfer between species, which causes oxidation and reduction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Look for which species loses electrons and which gains electrons, and explicitly connect that to oxidation and reduction in the reaction.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think redox electron transfer works like bond breaking and bond formation from organic chemistry, e.g. a bond in CdSO4 breaks first so it can bind to FeSO4.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer in redox is not explained by bond-breaking analogy alone; the correct explanation is based on electron movement and ionic species in solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Distinguish redox electron transfer from covalent bond rearrangement; identify the ions present and track electrons moving between oxidation and reduction partners.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe electrons travel freely through the solution in a redox reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are transferred from one species to another during oxidation-reduction; they do not simply travel freely through the solution as a separate moving entity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the reactant that loses electrons and the reactant that gains them, and describe electron transfer as a change in oxidation state between species, not free electron motion through solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The electrons travel freely through the solution"

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe sulfate carries electrons from one metal to another in the solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Sulfate is a spectator ion in the single-displacement redox reaction and does not carry electrons between metals; the electron transfer occurs between the reacting metal species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Separate spectator ions from the species undergoing oxidation and reduction; identify sulfate as present for charge balance, not as the electron carrier.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The sulfate carries the electrons from one metal to another"

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Nitrate attracts the metal into solution
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think nitrate's negative charge pulls the metal into solution or that nitrate is the active cause of the displacement.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate is a spectator ion in the Cu/AgNO3 reaction and does not drive the redox change; the redox process is between copper and silver ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify nitrate as unchanged in the net ionic equation and focus on the species that are oxidized and reduced.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The negative charge on NO3 attracts the metal into the solution"

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe nitrate receives electrons from one metal and passes them to the other.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate is a spectator ion and does not mediate electron transfer between metals in the reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Track only the species that undergo oxidation and reduction; ignore nitrate in the electron-transfer pathway because it remains spectating for charge balance.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Spectator ion as irrelevant because it cancels out
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a spectator ion is irrelevant simply because it cancels out in the net ionic equation, and therefore does not need conceptual attention.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A spectator ion may cancel in the net ionic equation, but it still has a structural role in the solution and should be recognized as a spectator ion rather than ignored conceptually.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine which ions remain unchanged across the reaction and separate them from the reactive species; understand why they are omitted in the net ionic equation while still present in solution.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Silver ions replacing missing charge on solid
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think two Ag+ ions replace the charge lost on the solid when Cu2+ leaves, treating charge as a physical object that gets filled in.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In the dynamic particle view, silver ions are reduced and deposited as silver metal while copper atoms/ions are oxidized; charge is not a material void to be filled.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Model the process at the particle level: ions approach, electrons are transferred, and atoms/ions change state; avoid treating charge as an empty space that requires replacement.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Cu2+ pulled into solution by nitrate because it has greater charge than Ag+
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think Cu2+ is pulled into solution by NO3- because Cu2+ has a greater charge than Ag+ and charge magnitude determines the motion.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The redox process is governed by electron transfer and electrochemical interactions, not by the idea that a higher-charge ion is pulled into solution by nitrate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Explain the displacement in terms of oxidation and reduction, identifying which species is oxidized and which is reduced, rather than comparing ionic charges as a cause of motion.

all_misconceptions.prevalence: 39.60% selected this alternative concept for item 17

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe two Ag+ ions are attracted to electrons left on the solid when Cu2+ leaves, implying a simple electrostatic filling of leftover electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions are reduced by accepting electrons during the redox process; the explanation should be based on electron transfer and deposition, not leftover-electron attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Track the transfer of electrons from the species that is oxidized to the species that is reduced, and describe deposition/reduction at the particle level.

all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and polyatomic ions must be distinguished correctly: sulfur in a compound has an oxidation number; sulfate is an ion with charge and constituent atoms with oxidation numbers.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students tend to lump oxidizing and reducing reagents together with many other reagents they memorize instead of classifying them by function.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidizing and reducing reagents should be identified as distinct functional categories based on the transformation they cause.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Brownish colour on iron is caused by addition of hydrogen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Rusting is an oxidation-reduction reaction in which iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust (hydrated iron oxides), not by hydrogen addition.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify rust as a chemical product formed when iron is oxidised in the presence of oxygen and water; the visible brown colour is evidence of rust formation, not hydrogen incorporation.

all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Rusting is oxidation of iron by oxygen in the presence of water; it is not a process in which carbonate catalyses reduction of iron.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Rusting of a metallic iron ship
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Rusting is the same as combustion because oxygen supports combustion and causes the iron to change colour.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Rusting is a redox corrosion process, not combustion; oxygen's presence does not automatically make the process combustion.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Rusting of a metallic iron ship
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Rusting is only a physical colour change, not a chemical redox process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Rusting is a chemical change involving oxidation and reduction, producing new substances such as rust.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should infer from the formation of a new substance and corrosion of iron that electrons are transferred and chemical composition changes.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The flame in combustion adds oxygen atoms to the copper metal, causing the blackening.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper blackens because it is oxidised by oxygen in air to form copper oxide; the flame is not simply adding oxygen atoms as a combustion feature.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect heating copper in air with oxidation of copper to copper oxide, recognizing the role of oxygen from the atmosphere and the electron transfer involved.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “combustion reaction has occurred because the flame outside the copper metal added oxygen” (077).

all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The black colour on heated copper is soot from the flame that dusts the copper surface.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The black colour is due to formation of copper oxide on the surface, not deposition of soot.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that heating copper in oxygen leads to surface oxidation, producing a black copper oxide layer rather than physical contamination by smoke.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the outside was made from black soot because the outside copper the smoke of the flame is black. It will dust the outside of the copper” (178).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Copper changes colour because it loses electrons, but this is not understood as oxidation/reduction chemistry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When copper is heated in air, copper atoms lose electrons to oxygen and are oxidised; this is a redox process.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect electron loss from copper with oxidation and electron gain by oxygen with reduction, identifying the overall process as redox.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “this is because copper lost electron and then changed colour” (153).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Copper turning black is due to addition of hydrogen, with oxidation as removal of hydrogen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating copper in air is oxidation of copper to copper oxide, not hydrogen addition/removal.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should base reasoning on oxygen uptake and electron transfer rather than hydrogen transfer in explaining the colour change.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “A redox reaction has occurred because there was an addition of hydrogen as reduction and there was removal of hydrogen as the oxidation” (175).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Copper was oxidised because oxygen was added to the metal during heating, but the process is not recognized as electron transfer or oxidation-state change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper oxidation should be understood as loss of electrons and increase in oxidation state, with oxygen acting as the oxidising agent.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use oxidation numbers and electron transfer together: copper goes from oxidation state 0 to +2 while oxygen is reduced.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred since oxygen has been added to the copper metal as oxidation” (066).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Copper envelope/frame heated in a flame
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Oxidation and reduction must balance each other so that the colour of copper remains maintained.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously in redox reactions, but they do not occur to maintain colour; they reflect electron transfer between species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that one species loses electrons while another gains electrons at the same time, and the observable colour change is due to new substance formation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred because both oxidation and reduction occurred simultaneously to balance each other thereby maintaining the colour of the copper metal” (113).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Carbon acts as a catalyst that reduces iron oxide by removing oxygen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon is the reducing agent in the blast furnace; iron oxide is reduced mainly through electron transfer, not by catalysis.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify that carbon/CO removes oxygen from iron oxide through redox chemistry and that a catalyst changes rate, not the overall products or reactants.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the carbon as a catalyst reduces Fe3O4 by removing its oxygen” (008).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 14.1% identified that carbon was a catalyst in the reaction
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron in iron oxide is oxidised because its oxidation number increases to form iron metal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron oxide is reduced to iron metal; iron's oxidation state decreases as it gains electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track oxidation numbers correctly from iron oxide to iron metal and recognize reduction as electron gain and oxidation-state decrease.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred because iron has gain in the oxidation number” (141).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron is reduced because it loses electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction is gain of electrons; iron oxide is reduced when iron species gain electrons and/or oxidation state decreases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should apply the rule that oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons, then check which species gains electrons in the blast furnace.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the iron has reduced because iron oxide has decreased in electrons …” (128).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide is reduced simply because oxygen atoms are removed from it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The process is a redox reaction in which iron oxide is reduced by electron transfer; oxygen removal alone is not the full explanation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should explain the role of carbon/CO as reducing agents and relate oxygen removal to the accompanying electron transfer and oxidation of carbon.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “oxygen is removed in the iron oxide to produce only the iron, so redox reaction has occurred” (101).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 26.8% identified that the iron oxide has simply reduced

all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide is oxidised by carbon to form iron metal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron oxide is reduced to iron metal while carbon is oxidised; carbon is the reducing agent.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the species losing electrons as carbon and the species gaining electrons as iron oxide/iron ions, showing coupled oxidation and reduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred because the iron oxide (Fe3O4) is being oxidised by the carbon into liquid iron” (207).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide is reduced because it changes its physical state or loses its properties as a metal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reduction in the blast furnace is a chemical change involving electron transfer and change in oxidation state, not a mere physical-state change.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish physical change from chemical reduction by identifying the formation of iron metal and the redox chemistry driving it.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “because iron oxide has changed from its original state to another iron oxide has lost it property as a metal to another state” (053).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide is reduced because of glaring light in the furnace.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reduction of iron oxide is caused by chemical reaction with carbon/CO under high-temperature conditions, not by light itself.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should focus on reactants and electron transfer rather than unrelated visible features like light intensity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “iron oxide has reduced; because the iron is running out with glaring means, the iron oxide has reduced” (182).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Carbon is the main reason iron oxide is reduced because a catalyst increases the rate of every reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon in the blast furnace is a reactant/reducing agent, not merely a catalyst; the reaction chemistry must be explained by redox processes.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that a catalyst is not consumed and does not determine product identity, whereas carbon is oxidised while iron oxide is reduced.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “carbon was a catalyst; because addition of a suitable catalyst increases the rate of every reaction” (011).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A redox reaction occurs because electrons are removed from a substance, without identifying which species loses or gains them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should identify the oxidation as electron loss by carbon/CO and reduction as electron gain by iron species in the blast furnace.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students need to specify the transferring species and connect electron loss with oxidation and electron gain with reduction in the overall redox reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a redox reaction has occurred because of the removal of an electron from a substance has occurred” (083).
all_misconceptions.population: 213 senior high school (SHS) 3 students in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Alternative Conceptions Associated With Application of Redox Reactions in Everyday Life

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reduction of iron oxide by coal/carbon
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Iron oxide decomposes into elements because coal is heated with it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blast furnace reaction is a redox reduction, not simple decomposition into elements.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not infer decomposition from heating alone; they should explain the conversion of iron oxide to iron through reduction by carbon/CO.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “iron oxide has decomposed into elements since the iron in the blast furnace is iron oxide and the coal (carbon) is necessary by heating” (162).

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Defining oxidation and reduction by hydrogen transfer
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat oxidation and reduction of organic compounds as movements of hydrogen only, rather than as changes in oxidation state that can also involve oxygen and other heteroatoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction in organic chemistry are determined by changes in oxidation state, often reflected by loss/gain of hydrogen and gain/loss of oxygen or other electronegative atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine bond changes and determine whether the carbon atom's oxidation state increases or decreases. Loss of H or gain of O/X increases oxidation state; gain of H or loss of O/X decreases oxidation state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Oxidation is the loss of hydrogen... Reduction is the gain of hydrogen..."

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Assuming oxidation always means adding oxygen and reduction always means removing oxygen
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation is only the addition of oxygen and reduction is only the removal of oxygen, ignoring other valid indicators such as hydrogen loss/gain or oxidation state changes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction can be recognized by changes in oxidation state; oxygen transfer is only one possible pattern, alongside hydrogen transfer and changes in bonding to electronegative atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the oxidation state of the carbon center before and after reaction, not rely only on oxygen addition/removal. If the oxidation state increases, the compound is oxidized; if it decreases, it is reduced.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Oxidation is the gain of oxygen... Reduction is the loss of oxygen..."

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Judging oxidation/reduction solely from numbers of bonds to oxygen or hydrogen
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may equate oxidation or reduction with simple bond-count rules only, such as counting C-O, C-H, or C-C bonds, rather than reasoning in terms of oxidation state changes at carbon.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond counting is useful only insofar as it helps determine carbon oxidation state; the real criterion is whether the oxidation state increases or decreases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should assign oxidation states to the relevant carbon atoms, track bond changes, and decide whether electron density around carbon increases or decreases. More bonds to oxygen or fewer bonds to hydrogen generally indicate oxidation, but the underlying concept is oxidation state change.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Thinking oxidation and reduction are simply changes in hydrogen or oxygen counts without oxidation state analysis
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may treat redox in organic chemistry as a bookkeeping problem of adding/removing H or O only, rather than determining whether carbon is oxidized or reduced by changes in oxidation number.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox classification depends on oxidation state: oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Equating oxidation number changes with only electron transfer and ignoring structural indicators
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think oxidation/reduction is only about explicit electron transfer and not about the structural changes that define oxidation state changes in organic compounds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In organic chemistry, oxidation and reduction are commonly inferred from changes in bonding to H, O, N, halogens, or C, which correspond to changes in oxidation state and electron density.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic observation of iron in copper(II) sulfate
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron does not react with CuSO4 / is insoluble in CuSO4, or that the visible change means iron simply dissolves like sugar in water rather than undergoing redox.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron displaces copper from CuSO4; the reaction is a redox process in which iron is oxidized and copper(II) is reduced, producing a reddish solution / copper deposit.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the observed color change to electron transfer and recognize that Fe(s) reacts with Cu2+(aq) to form Fe2+(aq) and Cu(s), rather than interpreting the observation as simple dissolution or no reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students with ability levels (-1.5 to 1.5 logit) are more dominant choosing the answer distractor B option (Iron does not react with CuSO4 solution)."
all_misconceptions.population: 1150 11th grade students from eight senior high schools in Eastern/Northern Sulawesi, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic observation of iron in copper(II) sulfate
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron is insoluble in CuSO4 because it is hard/solid, so they infer no chemical reaction from the visible evidence.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron undergoes oxidation in the reaction with CuSO4; the reaction is chemical, not dissolution based on hardness or physical appearance.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not infer reactivity from the physical hardness of iron; instead they should reason from the chemical changes and product formation expected in a displacement redox reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "iron is insoluble in CuSO4, due to the hard properties of iron."
all_misconceptions.population: Low-ability students in the macroscopic reasoning item analysis
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the net ionic equation can be written as Fe(s) + Cu(aq) → Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s), treating copper as neutral Cu(aq) instead of Cu2+ and/or omitting the ionic charge change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct net ionic equation is Fe(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify copper in solution as Cu2+ ions, then conserve charge and atoms while showing electron transfer from Fe to Cu2+.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students with low ability levels ... tend to choose the answer distractor C (Fe2+(s) + Cu(aq)→ 2Fe(aq) + Cu(s)) and B (Fe(s) + Cu(aq)→ Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s))."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron accepts electrons from CuSO4 instead of donating electrons to Cu2+.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron is oxidized by losing electrons; Cu2+ is reduced by gaining those electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track electron flow from Fe to Cu2+ and conclude that Fe is the electron donor and Cu2+ is the electron acceptor.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students with abilities ranging from -1.5 to 1.0 logit, tend to choose A (iron accepts electrons from CuSO4)."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi(Q2)
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Submicroscopic electron transfer in Fe/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the reaction between iron and CuSO4 is a redox reaction because of a generic idea of reaction occurrence, rather than because of electron transfer and oxidation-state changes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is redox because Fe is oxidized and Cu2+ is reduced through electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the electron-transfer model to justify redox classification, not merely the fact that two substances react.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students with low ability levels (less than - 0.5 logit) tend to choose C option (reaction of iron and CuSO4 is a redox reaction)."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the submicroscopic reasoning analysis of item 2sbAi(Q2)

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think zinc undergoes reduction when its oxidation number changes from 0 to -2.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc is oxidized in the reaction with CuSO4; its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers to reactants and products, then determine that Zn loses electrons and therefore its oxidation number increases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students' misconceptions, especially in understanding the changes in oxidation number of Zn (from 0 to -2), Zn experiences reduction."
all_misconceptions.population: Low-ability students in the symbolic reasoning analysis of item 6skBb
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation number changes in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students select oxidation-state options that place Zn or sulfate in incorrect oxidation states, showing confusion about how to assign oxidation numbers in the reaction equation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq), Zn goes from 0 to +2 and Cu2+ goes from +2 to 0; sulfate remains a spectator ion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers consistently to each species in the equation and identify only the species that actually change oxidation state.

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identifying the reducing agent in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think CuSO4 solution is the reducing agent in the reaction with zinc.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zinc powder is the reducing agent because it is oxidized and donates electrons; Cu2+ is reduced.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the species that loses electrons as the reducing agent and link that to the oxidation of Zn to Zn2+.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students argue that the reducing agent in the reaction between Zn and CuSO4 is a solution of CuSO4."

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identifying the reducing agent in Zn/CuSO4 reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse the role of products and reactants by thinking CuSO4 is the product of zinc undergoing reduction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: CuSO4 is a reactant providing Cu2+; it is not the product, and zinc is the reducing agent.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should classify substances by their role in the reaction equation and determine which reactant is oxidized and which is reduced.

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the metal is reduced and oxygen is oxidized in rusting.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Iron is oxidized and oxygen is reduced in the rusting reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should assign oxidation numbers before and after reaction to determine that Fe loses electrons and O gains electrons.

all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is not redox; it is a double displacement/precipitation reaction with no oxidation-state change.

all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Autoredox reaction of chlorine in water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO is a redox reaction in the generic sense of electron transfer, without recognizing it as an autoredox reaction of the same substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction is an autoredox (disproportionation) reaction because chlorine is simultaneously oxidized and reduced.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should see that the same element, chlorine, undergoes both oxidation and reduction in the reaction, so it is classified as autoredox.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "44% of students are sure that the reaction: Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO is a redox reaction, and 30% of students have reason that the reaction occurs because there is electrons transfer."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 44%; 30% gave the electron-transfer reason
all_misconceptions.source_title: The Development of Two-Tier Instrument Based On Distractor to Assess Conceptual Understanding Level and Student Misconceptions in Explaining Redox Reactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a reaction is redox only if oxygen is involved, and reject electron-transfer redox reactions that do not contain oxygen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox reactions can be defined by electron transfer, and oxygen transfer is only one special case.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify redox by asking whether electrons are transferred or oxidation states change, rather than whether oxygen is present in the reactants.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "MgO and Mg(OH)2 contain oxygen, what is absolutely necessary for redox reactions; to any redox reaction "O" is necessary – so choice (i) cannot be a redox reaction".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: about half of the students chose the correct answer (i); the remaining participants were not sure and chose (ii) or (iii) or both
all_misconceptions.population: several thousand secondary education students (Schmidt, 1994); cited in the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Macroscopic surface observation interpreted as sticking/gluing
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain the copper-colored coating on an iron nail as copper sulfate sticking, gluing, staining, or hanging on the nail like paint or wood color drying.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The copper coating forms because copper ions in solution are reduced to copper atoms that deposit on the iron while iron is oxidized into ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the visible coating to microscopic particle changes: copper ions gain electrons and become copper atoms that plate out, while iron loses electrons and enters solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper Sulphate sticks on the nail; it stuck, it glues on the nail like colour on a piece of wood and then dries up".
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students attribute the red copper deposit to attraction or magnetism caused by the iron nail.
