all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The deposit forms through electron transfer and redox chemistry, not magnetic attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that iron reduces copper ions in solution; the deposit results from chemical reduction, not physical attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Half of the students suspected an attraction as the cause of the red substance; other substance, other students mentioned an existing magnetism – probably because of the iron nail."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Half of the students suspected an attraction; other students mentioned magnetism
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Misuse of scientific terms without correct redox meaning
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can say things like copper dissolves, binds to iron, or copper atoms attract electrons, while still not correctly understanding the redox process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should use scientific terms consistently with the particle model: copper ions are reduced to copper atoms, and iron is oxidized.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should not just insert technical vocabulary; they need to explain electron gain by copper ions and electron loss by iron atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper dissolves from the sulphate and binds to the iron; Copper Sulphate is reduced: Copper atoms attracts electrons; iron nails can absorb the ionic solution".
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Black coating on heated copper is soot rather than copper oxide
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the black outside layer on heated copper is soot from combustion/fire rather than an oxide layer formed by reaction with oxygen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating copper in air forms copper oxide on the outside surface; this is a redox reaction involving oxidation of copper.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the black coating to copper reacting with oxygen in air, not to soot from burning, and should recognize oxidation of copper to oxide.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "by the flame/through combustion/fire is formed soot, burns outside the copper plate, copper oxidizes, the soot is copper II oxide".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 59% chose option B; only 21% gave the right answer (C)
all_misconceptions.population: students in the study on grades 10–12
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Combustion products explained as everyday-life soot/carbon products
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think oxygen is 'burned' and soot or carbon products are deposited, producing several everyday-life combustion products rather than a single oxidation product.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper is oxidized by oxygen; the process should be explained as a redox reaction with electron transfer / oxidation of copper, not as soot formation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the particle-level idea that oxygen in air oxidizes copper, forming copper oxide, and not invent combustion products like CO, CO2, or C as separate deposits.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxygen is burned and soot is deposited; oxygen is burned and carbon IV oxide is produced, the combustion leads to three products: CO, CO2, C".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Many students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Carbon as catalyst in blast furnace reduction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think carbon only acts as a catalyst or heat supplier and does not actually react in the blast furnace.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon is a reducing agent; it reacts with oxygen from iron oxide and is oxidized while iron oxide is reduced to iron.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that carbon removes oxygen from iron oxide, so carbon is consumed and oxidized rather than merely helping the reaction or supplying heat.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Carbon only helps to get the reaction going, but it does not react, carbon supplier the heat is necessary for the decomposition of iron oxide".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Mostly the answer (A) was chosen; correct answer (B) was only given by 20%
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iron oxide simply decomposes into elements when heated with carbon.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The process is a redox reaction in which iron oxide is reduced by carbon to iron, while carbon is oxidized.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify that oxygen is transferred from iron oxide to carbon, leading to reduction of the oxide and oxidation of carbon, not simple decomposition.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "carbon supplier the heat is necessary for the decomposition of iron oxide".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: The correct answer (B) was only given by 20% of the students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Writing balanced redox equations and half-reactions
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are unable to write correct equations for redox reactions, determine which species is oxidized or reduced, determine oxidation states, or write balanced oxidation/reduction half-reactions correctly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should determine oxidation states, identify electron loss and gain, and balance redox equations and half-reactions using conservation of mass and charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track electrons and oxidation numbers systematically to decide what is oxidized/reduced and then balance the half-reactions accordingly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Common areas of misconceptions include the students' inability to write the correct equation for reaction, determination which species is oxidized or reduced, determine the oxidation state of the species involved in the reaction, write a balanced equation for the reduction and oxidation half reaction correctly, or balance correctly a given redox equation."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Metal and ion level confusion in copper plating example
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students describe redox at the substance level rather than at the particle level, e.g., saying 'one Copper two ions takes two electrons and is reduced to Copper' without correctly linking it to copper atoms/ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox should be described at the submicroscopic level: copper ions gain electrons to become copper atoms, and metal atoms lose electrons to become ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish macroscopic substances from particles and explain reduction as copper ions gaining electrons to form copper atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one Copper two ions takes two electrons and is reduced to Copper": (instead of "to one Copper atom").
all_misconceptions.population: students at the beginning of their studies in chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Two Ideas of Redox Reaction: Misconceptions and Their Challeges in Chemistry Education

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Outer valence electrons are not part of a metal atom and do not affect its size.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Valence electrons are part of the atom/ion and contribute to its apparent size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that the outer electron cloud belongs to the atom; if electrons are lost or gained, the size of the species should change accordingly because the electron distribution changes.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the misconception that the valence electrons are not part of the atom was seen in student comments"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 6 students had difficulty interpreting whether the size of the metal atoms should include the transparent light grey sphere
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Valence electrons as forces or bonds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The valence electrons in a metal represent molecular forces or bonds rather than electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The transparent fuzzy region represents valence electrons, not a force or bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the visual cue as an electron cloud around the metal atoms, and distinguish electrons from the interactions that hold the metal together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Maybe that is supposed to represent the forces that make it a solid."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 17 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The red/white shapes represent nitrate ions, so nitrogen atoms are drawn as red and oxygen atoms are drawn as white.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The red/white shapes are water molecules in the more complex animation; nitrate ions are the blue/red clusters.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the key features of the animation and the chemical formula/structure of nitrate to identify species correctly rather than matching the color scheme to a remembered formula.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The nitrates. ... They are the two red with a white."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 28 of 55 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The blue/red clusters represent water molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blue/red clusters represent nitrate ions; water is represented by the large array of red/white shapes in the complex animation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify water by its abundant presence and molecular structure, and not confuse a nitrate ion depiction with water.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Water molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Cations and anions are attached or bonded together as ion pairs in water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When ionic compounds dissolve, the ions dissociate and exist as separate solvated ions in water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that water stabilizes separated ions through hydration, so the ions are not permanently bonded as neutral pairs in solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Just takes the copper [ions] and bonds it together with nitrate."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students thought ion-pairs would exist; 2 students viewing the simplified animation and 33 viewing the complex animation showed comments suggesting ion pairs
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: There are more silver ions than nitrate ions before the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In silver nitrate solution, silver and nitrate ions should be present in equal numbers before reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the formula AgNO3 and charge neutrality to infer a 1:1 ratio of Ag+ to NO3-.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There is too much water. I see mostly silver not much nitrate."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 14 students viewing the complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: There are more nitrate ions than silver ions before the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver and nitrate ions should be present in equal numbers before the reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that silver nitrate dissociates into equal numbers of Ag+ and NO3- ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Way more nitrates than silver."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Silver ions in this reaction have a +2 charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions in silver nitrate are Ag+ ions with a +1 charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the known formula of silver nitrate and charge balance to assign Ag+ rather than guessing a +2 charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Ten of these students believed that silver forms Ag2+ ions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Nitrate ions in this reaction have a -2 charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate ions are NO3- ions with a -1 charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply the formula of silver nitrate and the charge balance of the ions to determine that nitrate carries a single negative charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "five believed that nitrate exists as NO3 2- ions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Copper ions in this reaction have a +1 charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper is oxidized to Cu2+ ions in this reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from electron transfer and the balanced reaction that each copper atom loses two electrons, producing Cu2+ ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The responses from 32 of the 55 students showed a belief that copper forms Cu+ ions from this chemical reaction"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 32 of 55 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The charge of a cation is determined by counting the number of nitrate ions around it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A cation’s charge is determined by electron transfer and the chemical formula, not by counting nearby nitrate ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the oxidation-reduction process and ionic charges to infer the cation charge; nearby spectator ions do not determine charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Only if you can stop it to count the number of nitrates that are bonded to each"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reacting ratio of silver ions to copper atoms
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The silver ions and copper atoms react in a 1:1 ratio.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Two silver ions react with one copper atom; the reacting ratio is 2:1.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electron transfer and charge balance to see that one copper atom must supply two electrons to reduce two Ag+ ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It looks like 1 to 1 ratio in this."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: several students; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reacting ratio of silver ions to copper atoms
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The silver ions and copper atoms react in a ratio greater than 2:1.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Two silver ions react per one copper atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the balanced redox equation that the ratio must be 2:1, not 3:1 or 5:1.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It is like there are more silver, so like a 5 to 1 ratio. It is bigger than 2 to 1."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 7 of 55 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: When electrons are transferred from copper to silver, the charges of these species do not change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Losing electrons makes copper more positive and gaining electrons makes silver neutral; electron transfer changes charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect electron loss with oxidation and increased positive charge, and electron gain with reduction and loss of positive charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "no... I don't think the charge is changing"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: An unspecified number of electrons are transferred from copper to silver.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each copper atom transfers two electrons total, and each silver ion gains one electron.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the oxidation states and stoichiometry to determine that two electrons are transferred from one Cu atom to two Ag+ ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Not how many, but that it did."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 8 of 55 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Gaining or losing electrons will not change the size of an atom or ion.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron loss or gain changes the size of the species; Cu2+ is smaller than Cu atom and Ag atom is larger than Ag+ ion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that changing electron count changes electron-electron repulsion and effective attraction, altering ionic radius.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think it keeps relatively the same size"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 34 students stated sizes stayed the same; 39 of 55 discussed this issue
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Water molecules force the reaction to occur by bringing silver ions to the surface and pulling copper ions away from bulk metal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water is the solvent/medium; it does not drive the redox reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should treat water as the medium that solvates ions, while the driving force is the favorable electron transfer based on reduction potentials.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The water."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 35 students viewing the complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The behaviour of the nitrate ions drives this reaction because nitrate ions are more attracted to the copper ions than to the silver ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate ions are spectators and do not drive the reaction; the reaction is driven by redox electron transfer between Ag+ and Cu.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify nitrate as a spectator ion and focus on the electron-transfer chemistry between silver ions and copper metal.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it looks like the nitrates are forcing silver in and pulling copper out"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13 students made nitrate-driving comments; 4 of these held the stronger misconception
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The driving force for the reaction is a competition between copper and silver for nitrate ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The driving force is the greater tendency of Ag+ to be reduced by accepting electrons from Cu; nitrate does not determine the reaction direction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from standard reduction potentials and redox chemistry rather than from imagined attraction of metals to nitrate.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Copper must drive the silver away from the nitrate in order to bond with it."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The combination of copper and nitrate ions causes the blue colour in solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blue colour is due to aqueous copper(II) ions, Cu2+(aq).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the observed blue solution to hydrated Cu2+ ions, not to a copper–nitrate combination.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The copper released into solution and makes an ion with the nitrate and makes blue."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19 students in the demonstration; 8 students viewing the complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The blue sphere in the blue/red cluster is responsible for the blue colour in the aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blue sphere is a symbol in the particulate animation, not the cause of the macroscopic blue colour; the solution’s colour comes from Cu2+(aq).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the meaning of a visual symbol from the macroscopic property being represented and identify the actual source as copper(II) ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the blue thing is depicting the colour"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The blue sphere represents nitrate nitrogen and therefore nitrate is the source of the blue colour in solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrate is not the source of the blue colour; the blue solution is caused by Cu2+(aq).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the blue symbol in the animation is part of the nitrate depiction and not the macroscopic color source of the solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "So the nitrogen in the water is turning it blue."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 7 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The particulate depictions in the animations are a direct representation of the macroscopic properties of the substances present.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particulate symbols and macroscopic properties are different representational levels; symbols in the animation are not the same as observable properties.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between what is actually observed in the beaker and what is a symbolic particulate depiction in the animation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The belief that the blue sphere in the particulate view of the animation must be responsible for the blue colour of the solution ... are perfect examples of students conflating the macroscopic and particulate descriptions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described as a misconception; several specific instances given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student misinterpretations and misconceptions based on their explanations of two computer animations of varying complexity depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe ionic compounds dissolve in water as neutral molecules or as ion-pairs rather than as separated ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Solid ionic compounds such as silver nitrate dissociate into individual ions in aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: From the formula of an ionic compound and its behavior in water, students should reason that electrostatic attractions are overcome by hydration, producing free cations and anions rather than neutral pairs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the misconception that ionic compounds dissolve in water as neutral "molecules" or ion-pairs is well documented"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 of 55 students in the demonstration interview thought ion-pairs would exist; 8% of S group and 0% of CS group suggested ion-pairs; about 59% of C group and 62% of SC group suggested ion-pairs existed in solution.
all_misconceptions.population: 55 volunteer introductory chemistry students; groups S (n=26), CS (n=29), C, SC
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identity of water molecules in the complex animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misidentify the red/white shapes in the more complex animation as nitrate ions or as some other non-water species, rather than recognizing them as water molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The red/white shapes represent water molecules in the aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should match the visual model to the legend/chemistry context: red and white spheres depict H2O molecules in solution, while nitrate ions are blue/red clusters.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The most common mistake made when interpreting the red/white shapes was to identify them as nitrate ions."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 62% of C group and 54% of SC group correctly identified the red/white shapes; the remainder commonly misidentified them as nitrate ions.
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the more complex animation (C group and SC group)
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identity of nitrate ions in the complex animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the blue/red clusters as hydrated copper ions, blue molecules, or darker water molecules rather than nitrate ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The blue/red clusters represent nitrate ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that nitrate is the spectator ion shown as a blue atom with three red atoms; its presence does not indicate copper species or water molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students were more likely to misinterpret the blue/red clusters in the more complex animation as hydrated copper ions or as the object making the aqueous solution turn blue as the reaction occurred."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only 45% of the C group and 46% of the SC group correctly identified the nitrate ions; the rest misidentified them.
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the more complex animation (C group and SC group)
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Source of blue color in solution
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the blue color comes from nitrate ions, blue atoms in the nitrate cluster, or some other part of the animation, rather than from aqueous Cu2+ ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The solution turns blue because Cu2+(aq) ions form in solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the observed blue solution to the formation of copper(II) ions in aqueous solution, not to nitrate ions or water molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some of these participants referred to these blue/red clusters as nitrate ions, while others called them 'blue molecules' or 'darker water molecules'"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About 61% of C group and 66% of SC group incorrectly suggested water/nitrate-related sources of the blue color; many SC participants also said they could not identify any color change.
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the more complex animation, especially after viewing the more simplified animation (C group and SC group)
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Role of water in the reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe water molecules actively drive the reaction by pushing silver ions to the copper surface and pulling copper ions into solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water is the solvent and hydration environment; it does not force the redox reaction to occur or act as the driving force.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish solvation/hydration from reaction causation: water surrounds ions, but the spontaneous redox process is driven by electron transfer and redox potentials, not by water pushing particles around.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "these participants incorrectly believed that water was acting as the driving force for this reaction, forcing it to occur."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Approximately 61% of the C group and 66% of the SC group made this incorrect claim; 0% of the S group and CS group did so.
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the more complex animation (C group and SC group)
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the silver-to-nitrate ratio is not 1:1 in silver nitrate, especially after viewing the more complex animation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver nitrate contains equal numbers of silver ions and nitrate ions; the formula is AgNO3, so the ratio is 1:1.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the chemical formula of silver nitrate and conservation of charge to infer one Ag+ per one NO3- in solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "only 52% of participants in the C group correctly identified the silver-to-nitrate ratio, [but] 92% of participants in the SC group correctly identified this ratio."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 48% of C group did not correctly identify the 1:1 ratio; 8% of SC group did not.
all_misconceptions.population: C group and SC group students interpreting the more complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reacting ratio of silver ions to copper atoms
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the reaction occurs in a 1:1 ratio between silver ions and copper atoms rather than 2:1.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Two silver ions react with one copper atom in the redox reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should balance the electron transfer: each Cu atom loses two electrons, and each Ag+ gains one electron, so two Ag+ are needed per Cu atom.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Only 24% of the participants in the C group correctly identified the reacting ratio of silver ions and copper atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 76% of C group were incorrect; 85% of SC group were correct after seeing the simplified animation.
all_misconceptions.population: C group and SC group students interpreting the more complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer in the oxidation-reduction process
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to recognize that silver ions gain electrons and copper atoms lose two electrons, or they do not connect the two silver ions to the two electrons from copper.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions are reduced by gaining one electron each, and copper atoms are oxidized by losing two electrons each.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track electron conservation: one Cu atom provides two electrons, one to each of two Ag+ ions, producing Cu2+ and two Ag atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The adjusted least squares mean was 0.4 out of 4 for the C group participants, but was 1.6 out of 4 for the SC group participants."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: C group showed very low performance on the 4-point electron-transfer score; SC group performed better after the simplified animation.
all_misconceptions.population: C group and SC group students interpreting the more complex animation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Atom/ion size change on electron gain or loss
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize that silver ions get larger when reduced and copper atoms get smaller when oxidized.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When Ag+ gains an electron it becomes a larger neutral silver atom; when Cu loses electrons it becomes a smaller Cu2+ ion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason from charge and electron count that adding an electron increases the electron cloud size and removing electrons decreases it.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Almost all of the participants viewing the more simplified animation recognized the correct size changes"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Fewer participants viewing the more complex animation correctly identified the size changes; adjusted mean was 0.6/2 for C and 0.7/2 for SC, indicating frequent incorrect or incomplete understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the more complex animation (C and SC groups)
all_misconceptions.source_title: How does viewing one computer animation affect students' interpretations of another animation depicting the same oxidation-reduction reaction?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think sulfur and sulfate both have an oxidation number and a charge, rather than distinguishing oxidation number from charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An atom in a molecule/ion can have an oxidation number, while a polyatomic ion has an overall charge; these are different concepts.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species' overall ionic charge separately from oxidation numbers assigned to atoms within the species, and recognize that a polyatomic ion can have both an overall charge and oxidation numbers on its constituent atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "response D that sulfur and sulfate both have oxidation numbers and charges"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 13: 31.4% of GC1 and 28.2% of GC2 students chose response D; mean confidence 53.7% (GC1) and 56.3% (GC2).
all_misconceptions.population: GC1 (n=1083) and GC2 (n=510) general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Measuring meta-ignorance through the lens of confidence: examining students' redox misconceptions about oxidation numbers, charge, and electron transfer

all_misconceptions.subtopic: oxidation numbers vs charge in identifying redox
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify redox changes by tracking changes in the overall charges of polyatomic ions and molecules instead of oxidation numbers on atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox identification should be based on changes in oxidation numbers of atoms, not simply changes in the net charge of species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should assign oxidation numbers to the relevant atoms before and after the reaction and determine oxidation/reduction from changes in those oxidation numbers, rather than using changes in species charge as the criterion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They believed that the charge changed from -1 on NO3 to 0 on NO2 (i.e., oxidation) while the charge changed from +1 on H+ to 0 on H2O (i.e., reduction)."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 7: 34.2% of GC1 and 28.0% of GC2 students chose response D; mean confidence 54.0% (GC1) and 53.0% (GC2).
all_misconceptions.population: GC1 (n=1083) and GC2 (n=510) general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Measuring meta-ignorance through the lens of confidence: examining students' redox misconceptions about oxidation numbers, charge, and electron transfer

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons transfer as the bond between cadmium and sulfate breaks and as iron bonds with sulfate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons transfer from iron to cadmium in the redox reaction; the electron transfer is not caused by bond breaking/forming between cadmium and sulfate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the symbolic reaction to identify the oxidized and reduced species and then connect that to the particulate process: iron loses electrons and cadmium gains electrons, while sulfate is a spectator ion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students chose the response that electrons transfer as the bond between cadmium and sulfate breaks, and as the iron bonds with sulfate."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 10: chosen by 69.7% of GC1 and 68.6% of GC2 students; mean confidence 54.7% (GC1) and 60.0% (GC2).
all_misconceptions.population: GC1 (n=1083) and GC2 (n=510) general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Measuring meta-ignorance through the lens of confidence: examining students' redox misconceptions about oxidation numbers, charge, and electron transfer

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons transfer from cadmium to iron, from cadmium to sulfate and from sulfate to iron, or from iron to sulfate and from sulfate to cadmium, rather than from iron to cadmium.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In Fe(s) + CdSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cd(s), electrons transfer from iron to cadmium.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which element is oxidized and which is reduced by matching the reactants and products, then infer that electrons move from Fe(s) to Cd2+; sulfate remains a spectator ion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The remaining 70% of students preferred a response that electrons transferred from cadmium to iron, or from cadmium to sulfate and from sulfate to iron, or from iron to sulfate and from sulfate to cadmium."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only 33.2% of GC1 and 31.2% of GC2 students chose the correct response for question 9; about 70% chose one of the incorrect electron-transfer directions listed.
all_misconceptions.population: GC1 (n=1083) and GC2 (n=510) general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Measuring meta-ignorance through the lens of confidence: examining students' redox misconceptions about oxidation numbers, charge, and electron transfer

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students infer that because a spectator ion is adjacent to a cation in a chemical equation, a physical bond exists and electrons transfer by bond breaking/forming between the cation and spectator ion in aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Aqueous cations and spectator ions are not physically bonded simply because they appear adjacent in the symbolic equation; electron transfer occurs between the redox-active species, not by breaking/forming bonds with the spectator ion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the chemical equation using phases and ionic dissociation: (aq) indicates separated ions in solution, so adjacency in the written equation does not imply a real bond. They should locate electron transfer at the redox-active particles instead.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some students believed that the electrons transfer through bond breaking/forming between the cation and spectator ion because they saw the spectator ion direct adjacent to the aqueous cation in the chemical equation."
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed for ROXCI item development and general chemistry students responding to ROXCI items
all_misconceptions.source_title: Measuring meta-ignorance through the lens of confidence: examining students' redox misconceptions about oxidation numbers, charge, and electron transfer

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not know the proper charges of the silver, copper(II), and nitrate ions, and may think silver and copper ions have the same charge or the wrong charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions are Ag+; copper(II) ions are Cu2+; nitrate ions are NO3−.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the ionic charges shown in the animation or known from chemistry to identify each ion’s correct charge, then use charge balance to infer electron transfer and formulas.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "several students did not know the proper charges of the silver, copper(II), and nitrate ions"
all_misconceptions.population: college general chemistry students (interview comments from the study)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think silver and copper may gain or lose electrons but cannot determine how many electrons are transferred without explicit charge information; some infer an incorrect number such as two electrons for silver based on a wrong 2+ charge assumption.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each Ag+ gains 1 electron; each Cu atom loses 2 electrons to become Cu2+.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the initial and final charges of the species: Ag+ to Ag(0) means gain of 1 electron, and Cu(0) to Cu2+ means loss of 2 electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Aren't they both like 2+? Isn't A... isn't silver and copper 2+?"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Students whose animations depicted ion charges had 3.92 times greater odds of providing correct answers and 5.00 times greater odds of providing partially correct answers than those whose animations omitted ion charges.
all_misconceptions.population: interviewed students viewing animations without ion charges
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot tell how many electrons are transferred when electrons are shown as halos, and may not connect the 2:1 silver-to-copper reaction ratio to a 2-electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The animation should support counting transferred electrons directly: two electrons are transferred from one copper atom to two silver ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the number of electron symbols or, if using charge change, infer that one Cu atom loses two electrons that are gained by two Ag+ ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I just wouldn't know how many. I... So silver is gaining, so copper would be losing. Losing yeah. And... how many?"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Students viewing transferred-electron particles had 3.74 times greater odds of providing correct answers than students viewing halos.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a metal atom and its cation are the same size, or that the halo/electron depiction should not change perceived size.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A metal atom is larger than its corresponding cation because losing electrons reduces the ionic size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the animation’s size change and the idea that losing electrons to form a cation decreases electron-electron repulsion and overall size.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They look about the same. Yeah, there is not very much space in an electron though, so... Ha. They're about the same."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Students viewing transferred-electron particles had 16.01 times greater odds of demonstrating the misconception once rather than twice compared with students viewing halos; students viewing halos were more likely to consistently hold this misconception.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students write formulas for ionic compounds without using correct ion charges, for example treating copper nitrate as CuNO3 or assigning copper a negative charge to force balance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The balanced equation must use correct ionic formulas based on ion charges, e.g. Cu(NO3)2 for copper(II) nitrate and AgNO3 for silver nitrate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should determine the charges of the ions, combine them into electrically neutral compounds, and then balance atoms and charge across the full equation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Just the charges on the stuff. So the solid [metal] forms would be neutral, I think"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Students whose animations depicted charges scored 13.195/20 vs. 10.649/20 for students whose animations did not show charges.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.topic: Oxidation-reduction reaction of silver nitrate and copper metal
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may assign copper a charge of two-minus in the product and then propagate that incorrect charge into the formula and balancing process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper in copper(II) nitrate is Cu2+, so the neutral compound is Cu(NO3)2, not a negatively charged species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify Cu2+ as the cation, pair it with two nitrate anions, and then balance the overall reaction using neutral product formulas.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "That would be... two-minus. Then, hmm... That means it's [CuNO3] three-minus."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Does the way charges and transferred electrons are depicted in an oxidation-reduction animation affect students' explanations?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat oxidation-reduction as merely a transfer of symbolic charges rather than as a particulate-level electron-transfer process that changes species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox involves electron transfer between particles; symbolic charges and oxidation-state bookkeeping are representations of that process, not the process itself.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which particles lose electrons and which gain electrons, then connect the change in electron distribution to the observed oxidation and reduction of species. The written charges help track the process but do not replace a particulate explanation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "likely conceiving redox as merely a transfer of symbolic charges"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think oxidation-state changes are the same as the number of electrons rather than a bookkeeping of charge changes on species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation states are formal bookkeeping tools used to represent electron transfer; the actual chemical change is movement of electrons and resulting changes in species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine electron loss or gain, then use oxidation states to record the change in a way that conserves accounting rules; they should not confuse the oxidation state value with the number of electrons themselves.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It's the charge that's getting reduced. It's not the number of electrons."
all_misconceptions.population: Teacher 106's students, as discussed in micro-teaching
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the single-replacement equation means silver is literally 'kicked out' of the compound by copper as a symbolic swap in the written equation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Copper atoms oxidize and enter solution as copper(II) ions while silver ions are reduced and deposit on the copper lattice; the reaction mechanism is not a simple symbolic replacement of one species by another.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the particulate model to trace electron transfer: copper atoms lose electrons, silver ions gain electrons, and the observed products form by deposition and dissolution, not by a literal symbol swapping place in the equation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one 'kicks' one out of place"
all_misconceptions.population: Teacher 110 and the students being taught in micro-teaching
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think silver nitrate exists as bonded silver nitrate units in solution, with nitrate 'sticking' to silver instead of dissociated ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver nitrate in aqueous solution dissociates into hydrated ions; silver and nitrate are separate species surrounded by water molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize aqueous ionic compounds as dissociated ions, use particle-level evidence from the animation, and explain that water hydrates the ions rather than keeping them bonded as intact molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you're not necessarily gonna see that nitrate fall-you know-stuck to it"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think spectator ions are chemically participating in forming the redox products, rather than being nonparticipating ions present in solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Spectator ions remain in solution and do not undergo chemical change; they are omitted from the net ionic equation because they do not participate in the reaction mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the full ionic and net ionic equations, identify which ions change and which do not, and then omit unchanged spectator ions from the net ionic representation while still recognizing their presence in solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They're not actually participating in the production of formation of anything new."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the solid silver product is 'bouncing on top' of the copper because of surface placement in the animation, rather than recognizing it as deposited silver atoms/lattice formed by reduction of silver ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Silver ions gain electrons and deposit as metallic silver on the copper surface, forming a lattice while copper atoms are oxidized and leave the lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the visual deposition to reduction of silver ions and explain that the product is a new metal lattice formed from particles that gained electrons, not merely particles bouncing on the surface.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It's bouncing on top."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrated ions versus solid lattice species
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the species in redox are just the solid metal atoms or isolated formula units shown symbolically, without recognizing hydration or ionic state in solution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Redox in aqueous solution involves hydrated ions and metal atoms in a lattice; hydration state and phase matter for identifying the reacting species.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the particle depiction to distinguish solid lattice copper from aqueous hydrated silver and copper ions, and then track which species are actually oxidized or reduced.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "We know that the nitrate is there. We're gonna see it there when we kind of take a look at the animation."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume electrons transfer as a direct, localized one-step event implied by mnemonics or symbolic equations, rather than recognizing distributed changes across the copper lattice and surrounding particles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer in this redox system occurs through particulate interactions at different parts of the lattice and involves a sequence of events that cannot be reduced to a simple direct symbol swap.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the animation to trace where electrons are lost and gained, note that multiple particles and positions are involved, and explain the reaction as a mechanism rather than a one-step symbolic replacement.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "direct and localised electron transfer"
all_misconceptions.population: Discussed as a common implication of redox mnemonics and instruction in the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the mangle of teaching oxidationreduction with the VisChem approach: problematising symbolic traditions that undermine chemistry concept development

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Oxidation state change vs reaction type
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a reaction is a redox reaction because it is a combination reaction or because it has only one product, rather than because oxidation states change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction is redox only if oxidation states change; reaction type or number of products alone does not determine redox status.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare oxidation states of each species before and after the reaction. If at least one element's oxidation state changes, the process is redox; if oxidation states do not change, it is not redox regardless of whether it is a combination reaction or yields one product.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students with low person abilities tended to choose option A (i.e., that the process is a combination reaction) ... and fewer students with low person abilities chose options D (i.e., there is only one product)
all_misconceptions.population: First-year general chemistry students at a large public university (N=293 posttest; N=238 pretest; 209 both)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Examining the Psychometric Properties of the Redox Concept Inventory: A Rasch Approach

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electron transfer direction in aluminum/oxygen reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons are transferred from oxygen to aluminum in the aluminum and oxygen reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct reasoning is based on oxidation-state changes; the reaction is redox because oxidation states change, not because electrons move from oxygen to aluminum.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Assign oxidation states to aluminum and oxygen before and after reaction. Use the change in oxidation states to identify oxidation and reduction; do not infer the direction of electron transfer from a superficial reading of species names alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: fewer students with low person abilities chose ... B (i.e., there is a transfer of electrons from oxygen to aluminum) after the instruction.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Examining the Psychometric Properties of the Redox Concept Inventory: A Rasch Approach

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Role of aqueous ion in a redox reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the positively charged ion in solution is attracted to the site where electrons were deposited by the formerly neutral atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are directly transferred from the atom to the ion; the ion is not merely attracted to a site where electrons were deposited.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the electron donor and electron acceptor in the redox process. Reason in terms of direct electron transfer between species, not attraction to an electron-rich site.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: The majority of students tended to choose the distractor C (i.e., that the positively charged ion in solution is attracted to the site where electrons were deposited by the formerly neutral atom) rather than the correct response D (i.e., that electrons are directly transferred from the atom to the ion)
all_misconceptions.prevalence: majority of students
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the sample on item 16 (pre- and posttest trace plots)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Examining the Psychometric Properties of the Redox Concept Inventory: A Rasch Approach

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Association of oxidation numbers with atoms vs charges with compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students associate oxidation numbers with individual atoms and charges with compounds, rather than applying oxidation numbers appropriately to species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation numbers are assigned to atoms according to oxidation-state rules; charges are properties of ions or compounds as applicable, and students must distinguish oxidation number from overall charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use oxidation-state rules to determine the oxidation number of each atom in a species. Distinguish the oxidation number of an atom from the net charge of a compound or ion, and select statements consistent with those rules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: The proposed explanation for this trend is the tendency for students to associate oxidation numbers with individual atoms and charges with compounds
all_misconceptions.prevalence: dominant response over the entire range of person ability
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to item 8 (posttest trace plot)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Examining the Psychometric Properties of the Redox Concept Inventory: A Rasch Approach

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Recognizing redox while missing counterion role or electron-transfer mechanism
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can classify whether a process is redox but cannot consistently recognize the role of the counterion or the mechanism of electron transfer between the oxidant and the reductant.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: To fully understand a redox process, students should identify both whether redox occurs and how electrons move between oxidant and reductant, including the role of spectator/counterions where relevant.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine the redox classification using oxidation states, then analyze which species is oxidized and reduced and whether any counterion is merely a spectator rather than a participant in electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students in this sample were able to determine whether a process can be classified as redox but not to consistently recognize the role of the counterion or the mechanism of electron transfer between the oxidant and the reductant.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the sample, especially those answering items 10, 11, and 18
all_misconceptions.source_title: Examining the Psychometric Properties of the Redox Concept Inventory: A Rasch Approach

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize oxidation-reduction reactions in organic chemistry and do not spontaneously classify organic transformations as oxidation or reduction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Organic reactions can be analyzed as oxidation or reduction by comparing oxidation levels of reactants and products.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the structural change in the organic molecule and determine whether the product has a higher oxidation level (oxidation) or lower oxidation level (reduction) than the reactant.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students taking their first organic chemistry course often do not recognize oxidation—reduction reactions."
all_misconceptions.population: Students taking their first organic chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students tend to lump oxidizing and reducing reagents together with many other reagents they memorize rather than identifying them as oxidizing or reducing agents.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reagents in organic synthesis can be categorized as oxidizing agents or reducing agents based on whether they raise or lower the oxidation level of the organic substrate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first decide whether the transformation is oxidation or reduction, then select a reagent from the appropriate reagent class that accomplishes that change.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they tend to lump these reagents with the many other reagents that they memorize"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in first organic chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are reluctant to think in terms of oxidation when converting an alkene to an alkyne, especially when the synthesis passes through a single-bond intermediate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The conversion of an alkene to an alkyne can be understood as an oxidation because it increases the number of pi bonds from one to two.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that adding bromine to the alkene gives a dibromide intermediate at the proper oxidation state, and that the final elimination step is neither oxidation nor reduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There seems to be reluctance by students to proceed from a double bond to a single-bond intermediate when they are trying to generate a triple bond."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think every step in a multi-step synthesis must be an oxidation or a reduction, rather than recognizing that some steps are neither.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Some steps are neither oxidation nor reduction, even in an overall synthesis that includes an oxidation or reduction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate each step separately by oxidation level; if the oxidation level does not change, the step is neither oxidation nor reduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The final elimination step remains and is neither an oxidation nor a reduction."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not recognize that a rearrangement can be neither an oxidation nor a reduction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A rearrangement can occur without a change in oxidation state, so it should be classified as neither oxidation nor reduction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the oxidation level of starting material and product; if they are the same, no oxidation or reduction has occurred.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the product is at the same oxidation state as the starting material"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may assume tautomers necessarily differ in oxidation state.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Tautomers can have the same oxidation state.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the oxidation level of the tautomers rather than assuming structural rearrangement changes oxidation state; if all have the same oxidation state, no redox change occurred.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "all tautomers have the same oxidation state"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Comparing total oxidation numbers in balanced equations
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may overlook that the total oxidation numbers on both sides of a balanced organic equation must account for different numbers of molecules on each side.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When comparing total oxidation numbers, one must include the difference in the number of molecules reacting and formed in the balanced equation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should sum oxidation levels for all species on each side and adjust for unequal numbers of molecules so the totals match across the equation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the total oxidation numbers on both sides of the equation involves the difference in the number of molecules reacting and the number of molecules formed"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Which side gets the correction term
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not know that the extra oxidation-number adjustment is added to the side with fewer molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correction term is added to the side of the equation with the smaller number of molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count reactant and product molecules; the side with fewer molecules receives the additional oxidation-number unit(s) needed to balance totals.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I needs to be added to the total oxidation number on the side of the equation having the smaller number of molecules"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to account for bond formation or bond breakage when applying oxidation-number bookkeeping to organic reactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Even when bonds are formed or broken, oxidation-level comparison must still be balanced by considering the side with fewer molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the change in oxidation level across all products and reactants, including cases where the reaction changes the number of molecules, such as bond formation or bond cleavage.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "An example involving bond breakage is shown"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions in Organic Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think oxidation always means the literal transfer of real electrons from one atom to another.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation can be defined universally as an increase in oxidation state, and oxidation state changes may not reflect literal electron transfer in the mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine oxidation state changes from the formal rules; if oxidation state increases, the species is oxidized even when the mechanism involves atom transfer, nucleophilic displacement, or radical steps rather than direct electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "electrons are not always literally exchanged in redox reactions"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students infer that because oxidation/reduction half-reactions can be written, the reaction must occur by direct electron transfer at an electrode or via the written half-reaction mechanism.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Half-reactions are bookkeeping devices used to balance redox equations; they do not necessarily describe the actual reaction mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate formal balancing from mechanism: write half-reactions to track oxidation-state changes and electrons for stoichiometry, but examine mechanistic evidence to determine whether actual electron transfer occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it tells us nothing about the reaction mechanism"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think oxidation state is the same as formal charge or that oxidation-state changes correspond directly to formal-charge changes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation state is a formalism independent of formal charge; oxidation-state assignments can differ from formal charge and are based on electronegativity rules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should assign oxidation states using standard rules and not equate them with formal charge. They should recognize that oxidation-state changes may count electrons differently than formal charge does.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxidation states are independent of formal charge, valence, or bonding"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a higher oxidation state automatically means a stronger oxidizing agent.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation state does not directly determine oxidizing power; a species with a higher oxidation state can still be the poorer oxidant.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare actual oxidizing ability using thermodynamic or kinetic data, not infer it solely from oxidation state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "nitrate is the poorer oxidant"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any loss of hydrogen means oxidation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Only certain kinds of hydrogen loss indicate oxidation; loss of H: or H2 can be oxidation, but loss of H+ is not, and for H atoms the result depends on the electronegativity of the replacing atom and the oxidation-state change.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ask what form of hydrogen is lost and then determine oxidation states before concluding oxidation has occurred. If the oxidation state does not increase, the reaction is not oxidation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "loss of H+ is clearly not"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any gain of oxygen automatically means oxidation, regardless of whether other changes accompany it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Gain of oxygen indicates oxidation only when it occurs with no other accompanying change that offsets the oxidation-state change; oxidation should be identified by oxidation-state increase.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check whether oxygen addition is accompanied by another change, such as replacement by another electronegative atom, and then determine whether the relevant atom's oxidation state actually increases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "what is really meant ... in IUPAC definition III is gain of oxygen with no other accompanying change"
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory/general chemistry (implied audience of the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: oxygen or hydrogen as sufficient criteria
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely on the presence or loss/gain of oxygen or hydrogen as sufficient criteria to identify redox reactions, instead of checking oxidation-state changes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The central criterion for identifying redox in introductory chemistry should be whether oxidation states change.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first inspect oxidation states. If oxidation states do not change, the reaction is not redox; if they do, oxidation and reduction are present.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the very first thing to do in seeking to identify a redox reaction is to determine if any oxidation states change"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Oxidation and Reduction: Too Many Definitions?

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Charges on species in single-displacement reactions
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the charges on Zn, Cu, and NO3− do not change during the reaction Zn(s) + Cu(NO3)2(aq) → Zn(NO3)2(aq) + Cu(s).
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oxidation and reduction involve changes in oxidation numbers/charges for the species that are oxidized and reduced; Zn is oxidized and Cu2+ is reduced in the reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track oxidation numbers on the reactants and products. Elemental Zn starts at 0 and becomes Zn2+ in solution, while Cu2+ is reduced to Cu(s) at 0. Nitrate remains a spectator ion with unchanged charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The charge on Zn, Cu, and NO3− does not change in Zn(s) + Cu(NO3)2(aq) → Zn(NO3)2(aq) + Cu(s) [2A]"
